#91307. Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1048 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Natural Wonders: Crowley Lake Columns

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1048 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California.
  • Crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power.
  • Industry observers note that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It is low tide on Crowley Lake in Mono County, California. The water is still, the trout abundant, and one or two kayakers paddle about, enjoying the lack of tourists. But as you walk along the shore, something out of place appears: spiral pillars and arches that seem left over from some ancient civilization.

Crowley Lake is a man-made reservoir, administered by the Los Angeles Department of Water and Power. It was named after an important figure in the community, affectionately known as the Desert Padre. This beloved Catholic priest worked tirelessly to help a community that experienced water shortages throughout the 1920s and 1930s. Water from the nearby Owen Valley was diverted to Los Angeles, leaving very little for local residents.

Industry observers note that father Crowley made it his mission to bolster tourism in the area. The publicity led authorities to help locals by drawing up plans for a dam and reservoir. When Father Crowley died in a car accident, authorities completed the Long Valley Dam and named the reservoir Lake Crowley. If it weren’t for his intervention, the lake wouldn’t have existed.

As the years passed, visitors continued coming to Lake Crowley to fish, kayak, camp, and hike. Then something weird started to appear on the cliffsides. The banks appeared to be receding and hollowing out, revealing hundreds upon hundreds of spiral columns. Many onlookers believed they were man-made. Some compared the formations to Moorish architecture from North Africa and Spain.

Sources indicate that though the reservoir is man-made, the area’s history dates back millennia. Crowley Lake lies in the wider Long Valley Caldera, one of Earth’s largest calderas.

Some of the columns. Photo: Shutterstock.

The caldera sits atop one of three ancient supervolcanoes in the United States. Around 760,000 years ago, this supervolcano erupted and spewed 650 cubic kilometers of rhyolite rock and ash into the air for a week. It covered the land in a blanket of ash and debris over one kilometer thick. And it left behind a 32km long, 18km wide, and 900m deep depression in the earth.

It has been revealed that the depression formed when the subterranean magma chamber emptied onto the surface and the remnant shell of a roof collapsed. The blast and pyroclastic flow were so powerful that ash fell as far as Kansas. Along the rim are the lava dome complexes of Mammoth, Glass, and Bald Mountains. The caldera also hosts a cluster of hydrothermally active lakes called the Mammoth Lakes.

The main feature left by the eruption is the Bishop Tuff, a few square kilometers in area. A tuff is a rock of compacted volcanic ash. At the base of this tuff stand the Crowley Lake Columns. They range in thickness, average about six meters high, and are generally reddish, beige, grey, or white with a dark water line at their base. Some lean while others stand straight.

Attached by arches, the columns are so evenly spaced that to some visitors, it resembles an ancient temple. Horizontal cracks about 30cm apart add further detail to the columns. They look like they hold up the cliffs but they simply remained after the softer cliff rock started to erode.

Industry observers note that the high levels of silica, sodium, and potassium in the columns make the rock conduct heat well and cool suddenly. This led to the cracks. Similar formations exist in Guatemala, Mexico, and Upcoming Mexico.

Sources indicate that the few people who frequent Crowley Lake have long known about the columns. Only recently, social media has started to highlight them. This is due to its seclusion on the lake’s shoreline. The only ways to access them are on foot or by boat, kayak, or 4×4. The dirt road on which you turn from Highway 395 is so steep and uneven that it can bog down vehicle. Visitors tend to drive halfway, then walk.

Despite popular speculation that these columns are an example of columnar jointing, they are not. The geological process is different. With columnar jointing, the spaces are not so far apart. A study by geologists at UC Berkeley used a combination of computer models, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscope imagery to determine how they formed. It turns out that the culprit is simply…water.

“We hypothesize that the columns are a result of instabilities at the liquid water and steam interface as cold water seeped into the still-cooling Bishop Tuff,” notes Noah Randolph-Flagg, the study’s lead scientist.

Recent findings suggest that the columns formed through hydrothermal convection. Photo: Shutterstock.

Essentially, rainwater seeped down into the hot ash and started to boil, producing a mineral glue called mordonite. The boiling water formed a column of steam which carried the mordonite upward through the rock. Thus, the mineral hardened the rock, leading it to remain standing while the surrounding rock eroded. This process is called hydrothermal convection or circulation.

Industry observers note that according to Randolph-Flagg, it only took 100 years to form these columns. The study also states that “the liquid water–steam interface probably is the source of the instability that generates columnar flow.”.

As for the erosion of the cliffside, the reservoir’s water levels fluctuate throughout the year with the seasons. After the completion of the reservoir, the columns started to reveal themselves. The constant rise and fall as well as a repeating freeze-thaw cycle caused the tuff to recede. It revealed the columns and also hollowed out the cliffside to form shallow caves. Take care when going into these little caves or pushing on the columns, as they might not be as stable. As the cliff continues to erode, we should see more of these columns.

The arches resemble Moorish architecture. Photo: Shutterstock.

In terms of the Long Valley Caldera, scientists have closely monitored its activity, which has been increasing since the 1980s. Since it is a one of only 20 supervolcanoes in the world, they have paid close attention to its potential for eruption, despite its status as inactive.

In a recent development, there have been small earthquakes and signs of movement in the earth as if it were “breathing.” This is seen in Yellowstone, another supervolcano. While there are no immediate signs of an impending eruption, the caldera’s history and current activity suggest that it is possible.

#91302. Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (512 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (512 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

“It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

On a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

According to recent reports, “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

It has been revealed that vasiliev noted that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Baia says the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

Recent findings suggest that on Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no upcoming soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Sources indicate that yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

Recent findings suggest that the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#91298. Latest Update: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1292 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • Sources indicate that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing new route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

Sources indicate that in the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin noted. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

Bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” remarked Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

Industry observers note that for Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he mentioned.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

If your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

Sources indicate that the team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Sources indicate that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson said. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” mentioned Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

Recent findings suggest that that remarked, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Industry observers note that buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they said. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

In a recent development, once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the major cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

Sources indicate that to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

In a recent development, conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

Marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

In a recent development, “That is why it is crucial to consider all options and potential problems before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

Asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

Industry observers note that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they mentioned. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

Industry observers note that they warn that conditions in the Andes are changing quickly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles noted. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Industry observers note that sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he remarked.

It has been revealed that the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they stated.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • According to recent reports, according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

According to recent reports, according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

According to recent reports, the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

It has been revealed that “He was really lucky,” said Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

According to recent reports, by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

Weekend Warm-Up: Behind the Climb

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • It has been revealed that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

It has been revealed that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

Recent findings suggest that the Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Industry observers note that hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Industry observers note that interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

In a recent development, ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed strategy.

Recent findings suggest that despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

In a recent development, keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • According to recent reports, the journey has not gone according to plan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin launched his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

According to recent reports, the journey has not gone according to plan. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

Industry observers note that while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

According to recent reports, given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid prepares. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

According to recent reports, but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Industry observers note that roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

In a recent development, for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

It has been revealed that by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and strategy ahead.

Sources indicate that the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line reveals the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

Industry observers note that I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

In a recent development, I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

According to recent reports, food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

Recent findings suggest that safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

Industry observers note that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

It has been revealed that we have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

Successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

Sources indicate that you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

In a recent development, we were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

According to recent reports, there is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

In a recent development, back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

University changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

The decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

The actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

Sources indicate that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

#91286. A Desk Jockey Passed on 40 Brown Bears. The 41st Charged

A Desk Jockey Passed on 40 Brown Bears. The 41st Charged

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4143 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The 41st Bear,” appeared in the September 1961 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • According to recent reports, john Yenter turned away from a 20X spotting scope and looked me right in the eye.
  • It has been revealed that I had just refused to go after the 39th bear that failed to meet my specifications, and John, my hunting partner, was again giving me a piece of his mind.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The 41st Bear,” appeared in the September 1961 issue of Outdoor Life.

According to recent reports, john Yenter turned away from a 20X spotting scope and looked me right in the eye. He stated, “Bill, you’re absolutely crazy. Forget your foolish specifications and collect that bear. You’re acting like a decrepit old desk hand, not a hunter.”.

It has been revealed that I had just refused to go after the 39th bear that failed to meet my specifications, and John, my hunting partner, was again giving me a piece of his mind. He never uses profanity, but he can do a blistering job without it. He had killed his bear like an expert, and now I, the junior member, was giving him trouble. Being six years older than I am, he felt perfectly justified in straightening me out.

Sources indicate that it started months ago back in York, Pennsylvania, where my job — director of purchases for a large manufacturer of air-conditioning equipment — classifies me as a professional desk hand. I guess I look the part — gray, balding, and past several of man’s milestones.

My business associates in Borg-Warner are fond of trying to decide whether I was born a penny-pincher, which made me a purchasing agent, or the other way around. While they were debating that problem, I was concentrating on a 60-day toughening-up routine of golf, bowling, hiking, and calisthenics to convert my body from paper-shuffling to hunting condition. This was notable because John C. Yenter, a building contractor from Tyrone, Pennsylvania, and I were planning a Kodiak bear hunt. We had so completely enjoyed our polar bear hunt in Norway’s frozen arctic region (“Desk Hand vs. Polar Bear,” Outdoor Life, December, 1957) that John decided his work with West Virginia Pulp & Paper Company could wait while we took a brown-bear hunt.

According to recent reports, I wrote down some rigid specifications for my trophy brown bear and made a silent vow to live up to them. I wanted a male with a 10-foot-square hide, brown in color, a perfect pelt, and weighing 1,000 pounds or more.

Research indicated that Kodiak Island raised the largest, brownest bears, and a spring hunt would be my best bet for a trophy with a full-grown, unrubbed pelt. The idea was to get a bear fresh out of hibernation — before he ruined his pelt with mating-season fights or started to shed his winter coat. We scheduled our hunt for late April and early May, which appeared to be the prime time for Kodiak brownies.

Recent findings suggest that we met our outfitter, Alf Madsen, in Kodiak Village, on April 27. We knew that most Kodiak bear hunting is done from the salt-water bays around the island, but records show that more massive bears are taken in the interior. So we were bound for Karluk Lake, in the center of the southern part of the island.

Sources indicate that the flight up the valleys, around and between the snow-covered mountains, was a sight so beautiful that we almost forgot we were in a little single-engine pontoon plane and at times many miles from any water to sit down on. We were in camp and ready to hunt on the morning of April 28.

In a recent development, our camp consisted of one frame cabin, one tent cabin, and an outhouse, without door, 100 yards north on the main bear trail. All the camp equipment, including two outboard boats for lake travel, had been flown in.

Industry observers note that karluk Lake looked a lot like one of the fjords of Norway. The blue water of the lake was now entirely clear of ice, but there were deep snowdrifts on the mountain peaks above the lake. If we’d never seen a bear, the wild beauty of the place would have repaid me for the trip in full.

We started the hunting campaign with all energy, and in two days we saw and classified 16 bears. I refused to stalk any of them because they failed to meet my specifications. John eventually suggested that I was displaying the stubbornness of a mule, rather than the calm judgment of a purchasing agent.

In a recent development, our guides were by reputation the best on the island, and they soon proved that they deserved their standing. Some would call them Aleuts, but in reality they were members of the Koniaga Tribe, which has been considerably diluted by the Russians who owned the island until we bought Alaska from Russia in 1867. Our guides were proud of their Russian and Koniaga lineage, but they’re loyal United States citizens.

Industry observers note that my guide was Grishka Nicoli, and John’s was Nick Malutin. These guides spoke their native Koniaga language, which is spoken only and not written. They also spoke fluent Russian and awkward English. They spend about three months of the year as hunting guides and four months as commercial salmon fishermen. For the rest of the year they’re Koniaga gentlemen of leisure. Like my hunting partner John Yenter, the guides were convinced that I was entirely too meticulous in my trophy specifications.

The only encouragement I had came from Kim Clark, who had become a very important part of our expedition. His full name was Webster Kimberly Clark, and he was a refuge biologist employed by the U. S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Kim had been reared in Greenfield, Massachusetts, had studied at the universities of Michigan, Massachusetts, Missouri, and Yale. He has a Doctor’s degree. Clark had done a vast amount of field research and had become one of the top authorities on North American bears. He was stationed on Kodiak Island by the federal government to study Kodiak bears.

Recent findings suggest that kim Clark had read my stories in Outdoor Life.* When Kim learned from outfitter Alf Madsen that I was planning a Kodiak hunt, he met me in Kodiak Village and asked if he could join the group to observe and record the data on bears killed. We were glad to have a man of his ability and knowledge.

In a recent development, during the early part of our stay on Karluk Lake, Kim worked alone and permitted us to hunt as hunters, not as scientists. He was a great addition to our expedition, because his lectures at night permitted us to do practical field work the next day in connection with our hunt. Between hunting, field and night classes, we were extremely well occupied.

Had it not been for Kim encouraging me to stick to my specifications, I might have given up. He encouraged me because accurate field data on a massive male brown bear just out of hibernation is apparently very scarce.

By the third day my partner John was adjusting his own specifications to suit the bear that was in sight. We were glassing a brownie on the shoreline across the lake, and through the glasses it looked good — perfect hide, pleasing color, but slightly under my requirements as to size. John wanted it.

In a few minutes we were on our way across the lake, approaching very quietly so as not to alarm the bear. We landed several hundred yards from the bruin, and John started stalking the animal with his guide. In spite of the skill they displayed, the bear caught the man smell. He was on his way up the mountainside before John could shoot. He and Nick stood on the shore watching the occasional motion of a bush which indicated that the bear was going higher and away.

The bear was 150 yards from the lake shore when he came into a little opening in the brush where we could see him. At that point he made the biggest and last mistake of his life. He stopped and looked back. At that moment John fired. The bear fell. Two more shots finished him completely. John’s performance was a credit to him, to his .375 H. & H. Winchester, Model 70 rifle, and its Bausch & Lomb scope sight.

It was without question a major bear, the color was excellent, the 8½-feet-square hide was prime and perfect. John was a thoroughly happy hunter.

With his bear hide strung up to dry, John concentrated on the wonderful trout fishing near camp, with time out now and then to think up some upcoming criticisms of my ideas about a proper trophy.

At the end of the ninth day we sized up the situation and found that we had glassed 40 bears, killed one. I was still holding out for a bigger and better one.

The weather was perfect for the first three days, which was probably why we saw so many bears. There was rain every day after that, and visibility was often too poor for good work with binoculars. There’s no climate on Kodiak, just a vast assortment of unexpected and undesirable weather.

It has been revealed that when we started out the 10th morning, we found that what had been rain at the lake camp during the night had been snow above the 1,500-foot level on the mountain. In spite of that, our hunting began early, and at 8:30 we saw a bear that looked very interesting. He was a mile from the lake shore, 1,600 feet higher, just above the new but temporary snow line.

Industry observers note that trying to get a better look at the bear, we moved up the bed of Cottonwood Creek. This took us out of sight of the bruin momentarily, but we knew exactly where he was because the snow line established his elevation and the pass made in the mountains by the creek marked his location the other way. Yet, an hour’s looking from our fresh position failed to locate him.

In a recent development, we then climbed up high on the right bank of Cottonwood Creek, and from there we glassed constantly until noon. We felt sure that the bear was there because we certainly would have seen him if he’d walked away.

At noon we abandoned that position and moved to a spot across the lake, a mile farther away, which gave us a better perspective and a view of more of the ground area. We took turns eating and resting, but we were constantly looking. The rain returned in full force and it was a very uncomfortable situation.

We never saw a sign of the bear until 4 o’clock, when suddenly he stood up and was in plain view again. It was now evident that we’d first seen him when he finished his morning feeding, and he’d bedded down for the day. Now he was up feeding again.

Recent findings suggest that after a few minutes of careful observation, the guides decided that this bear would meet every point in my specifications. This was a fine display of skill on the part of the guides and is something I could never hope to duplicate. To the inexperienced, a bear two miles away through a 20X Bausch & Lomb telescope is just a bear, but my guide was able to classify him very accurately as to sex, size, and condition.

I knew enough by now to trust this guide’s judgment, and in a few minutes we were on our way back across the lake to start the stalk.

Before we reached the far shore the clouds had dropped so low that the mountains were completely obscured.

It has been revealed that since John had killed his bear, we decided that he’d stay with the boat and the two guides would accompany me on the climb up the mountain. It took a few minutes to strip for action, which meant down to heavy underwear, a sweat shirt, rain suit, and hip boots. This sounds like unusual mountain-climbing equipment, but the first mile of our climb would be accomplished by wading up the creek. It was much easier that way than climbing through the murderous alder thickets on either side.

By 5:30 we’d accomplished the most difficult part of the climb and were at about the same height as the bear and 500 to 800 yards to the right of him. At this point we climbed out of the creek and dived into the alder thicket. All alder thickets are nasty, but this one was the worst that I’d ever seen.

Sources indicate that soon we picked up a prominent bear trail, a path so worn that one of the guides called it “a bear highway.” It was obviously the main bear trail on that particular mountainside, and we felt sure that my bear was on it. We had no idea which way he was traveling, so it was possible that we’d meet him at any moment. It was also possible that he’d park a few yards off the trail to observe and properly take care of anything that might be using the bear highway. It’s this kind of thinking that prevents daydreaming on brown-bear stalks.

It has been revealed that grishka, who was in front of me, explained that he’d lead and watch ahead. Nick would bring up the rear and watch behind us and to the sides of the trail. I was free to watch any angle that suited my fancy. I think this was a polite way of telling me that they didn’t trust my powers of observation.

I was planning what I’d do if certain things happened. I realized that any shooting would be at very close range because of the thick alders and the heavy fog. While my guides were both carrying .348 Winchesters with open sights, I was carrying a .375 Winchester with a Bausch & Lomb scope. No scope is ideal equipment for a quick shot at 10 yards, and I wished for an old-fashioned V notch and front post.

Industry observers note that nick must have been reading my mind. He mentioned, “Bill, if we meet the bear and you have trouble with your rifle, just throw it down and grab mine. I’ll be right behind you.”.

According to recent reports, nothing could have done me more harm than that speech. I knew now that he had no more confidence in my equipment than I had, and I was scared stiff. I had enough acid in my stomach to pickle a ton of iron castings.

We soon came out into the little open spot on the mountainside that we’d marked as the location of the bear when last seen almost two hours before. This clearing was about 100 feet in each direction — no alders, just dead grass almost knee high. We spent 20 minutes searching the open area and forcing our way into the brush around the edges, trying to pick up a trail or some sign of the bear.

Suddenly my head was gripped by Grishka, a powerful man but only five feet tall. He pulled my head down to his level, slapped his wet face against mine. Pointing to the right, he whispered in my ear, “Bear there. Shoot!”.

According to recent reports, about 75 yards away, through a little opening in the brush, I could see a dark spot. It could have been a bear. As I dropped to one knee, my perfect guide braced his knees to my back to steady my position. His 9X binoculars were tight to his eyes and just above my head as he watched the bear.

When I picked up that brown spot in my 2½X scope, I couldn’t tell whether it was a bear or not. If it was, I couldn’t for the life of me see which way he was pointing.

In a whisper, I asked Grishka, “Which end is the head on?”.

After a full minute’s careful observation through his glasses, he put his mouth to my ear and remarked, “Other end. Shoot!”.

That concise data from Grishka was fed through my fire-control center down to the trigger finger, and my gun fired. I was so excited I didn’t hear the report of the rifle, nor was I conscious that there was any recoil. But I did hear the bullet hit something, and then a fraction of a second later I knew it was a bear. He roared his complete disapproval of the whole situation.

Then it seemed that the brown bulk went up in the air several feet. An instant later it was on the ground and for a split second was completely still. At that moment I fired my second shot, and the bear’s reaction to that was a quick lunge to the right, toward the alders. I fired my third shot as he disappeared.

Grishka had said the first shot was good, but I didn’t see how he could possibly know. The bear had disappeared into the brush just as though he hadn’t been touched.

It has been revealed that both guides were now running as hard as they could to the right — in the same general direction the bear was going when we last saw him. It was quite obvious that they were attempting to get ahead of the bear before he reached the creek bed, which was 600 yards away. I caught them rapidly and stayed right with them, not due to any bravery on my part, but simply because it was obviously much safer to stay close to them and their two rifles.

Our travel in the next few minutes was parallel to that of the bear, and we could follow his location by the noise he made. I thought — and hoped — that the amount of noise was due to the fact that he was badly wounded, running blind and knocking brush to one side.

Sources indicate that A few seconds later we were on the edge of the creek where we could look down a steep bank to the water 100 feet below. Then I realized that the noise of the bear was not to my left, as it had been, but almost back of me and getting closer. I turned to face the noise. A second later that bear came into sight less than 20 yards away.

According to recent reports, it was the most stirring sight a thrill hunter could ever hope to see. That bear was coming at us at top speed, and it looked as though he knew exactly what he was going to do when he got there.

I slammed the gun to my shoulder and looked at the bear in the scope sight. The contour of the ground was such that I could see the back of his neck, so I selected a spot where the neck joins the shoulders. The crosshairs settled on that spot. I tightened on the trigger, adding pressure and waiting for the recoil.

But the bear rolled dead as Caesar before my rifle went off. I lowered the weapon still cocked and loaded. I never have felt so cheated in all my life. In another 1/10th of a second I could have been the Man Who Stopped the Charging Brownie.

Later examination revealed that the first shot had gone very effectively into his side just back of the ribs, forward under the spine, just grazing it, cutting the main blood vessels just back of the heart. Clearly the bear had been too far gone to make a determined charge. He was only making a blind run with his last spark of life, and we happened to be in his path.

That bear was coming at us at top speed, and it looked as though he knew exactly what he was going to do when he got there.

Recent findings suggest that I examined the bear closely, and was glad that I’d stuck to my specifications. It was a male, the color dark brown, the hide in perfect condition, and the size was enough to flatter any desk hand. It was the 41st bear we’d seen on this trip.

Suddenly I realized that it was beginning to get dark. We’d have to leave the bear and return the next day to do the skinning. I was worried about what might happen to the hide overnight, but Grishka stated, “We leave strong man smell here. Nothing bother.” With a grin he added, “The strongest thing here is white-man smell of your sweat shirt. We leave it.”.

Industry observers note that I peeled off the shirt and he tied it to a limb above the bear. When we returned the next morning the shirt and the bear were there and nothing had bothered it.

The guides, Kim Clark, and I left camp early next morning and climbed the mountain to skin the bear. John remained in camp. He and the cook, Pete Unger, had planned a fishing trip.

It has been revealed that kim was keenly interested in the bear from our description so we went in loaded with camera equipment, scales, surgical instruments, test tubes, and specimen bottles. Very few Kodiak bears have ever been accurately weighed and examined, and this is especially true of significant bears just out of hibernation.

Sources indicate that my bear was an ideal specimen for studying the effects of hibernation, because he evidently had just come out of that lethargic state. The stomach was found to be about 1/10 full, and the contents weighed 16 pounds. Carefully separated and weighed, we found that the contents were 55 percent blue-joint grass, 20 percent nettle, 20 percent wild celery, and 5 percent poque, which is a parasitic growth on the roots of the alders. There was no animal matter present.

Recent findings suggest that the intestine was then examined and the length was accurately determined to be 77 feet 6¾ inches. It was then split from end to end for internal examination. There was no food in it. This indicated two things: first, that the bear had not been out of hibernation long enough for food to pass through the stomach into the intestine, and second, that he had gone into hibernation with the intestine completely empty, which conformed to the generally accepted theory. Further examination revealed there wasn’t a sign of ulcer, scar, scab, or scale in the stomach or intestine.

Recent findings suggest that we also observed that there were no parasites of any kind in the entire digestive tract. This is one of the strange results of hibernation, because this bear during the six months of feeding eats carrion of all kinds, specializing in dead fish. He also digs up and eats worms, insects, and roots. When winter comes, he’s literally and actually a fur coat full of worms. There are thousands of them, including 10-foot-long tapeworms. The bear knows instinctively that he cannot go into hibernation with any food in his body; it would ferment and cause serious trouble before spring.

Industry observers note that so when winter approaches he goes on a bedtime diet of certain plants and berries. Then, after a few days of fasting, he’s completely empty. The worms go with the food, and he goes to sleep physically clean. His stored body fat keeps him going till spring.

Every piece of this bear was carefully weighed. He weighed 840 pounds at the time he was killed. Kim Clark figured his weight when he was fattened for hibernation in the fall would have been about 1,300 pounds.

Sources indicate that his age was estimated at ten years. The rough field measurement of the skull indicated a Boone and Crockett rating of 28½, against the world record of slightly above 30 inches. Unless the skull shrinks more than an inch during the drying period that must precede official scoring, the trophy should rate a place on the Boone and Crockett record list. This was in every respect an outstanding bear. I learned a lot from him, and much more from Kim Clark.

The skull and all the data collected were sent to Dr. Robert Rausch, Arctic Health Research Center, Anchorage, Alaska, where it became a part of their records.

Read Next: We Stalked a Cannibal Brown Bear That Was Trying to Kill a Cub.

Recent findings suggest that we were glad to work with Dr. Kim Clark and Dr. Rausch, but in a way it was unfortunate. I can’t enlarge on the size of this bear as the years roll on and the hunt becomes a fond memory. This is one Kodiak that will never experience any post-mortem growth.

Sources indicate that *H. L. Consley, who has become known to Outdoor Life readers as the Desk Hand, is the author of “Desk Hand in the Yukon,” in the January, 1956, matter; “Desk Hand Afloat,” November, 1956; “Desk Hand vs. Polar Bear,” December, 1957, and “Desk Hand in the Arctic,” August, 1959.

#91282. Trophy Deer Hunting Is a Trap

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1060 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Trophy Deer Hunting Is a Trap

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “The Trophy Trap,” was originally published in the November 2006 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • It has been revealed that it was almost 40 years ago that the first whitetail came into my life.
  • Industry observers note that finally, I had entered the cadre of hunters who had taken a whitetail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “The Trophy Trap,” was originally published in the November 2006 issue of Outdoor Life.

It has been revealed that it was almost 40 years ago that the first whitetail came into my life. I dropped him on a granite ridge in New York’s Hudson River Valley, where, on a clear day, you could see the Empire State Building 40 miles away. The buck was only a forkhorn, but I was beside myself with excitement.

Industry observers note that finally, I had entered the cadre of hunters who had taken a whitetail. In those days, that feat often took some doing.

According to recent reports, back then, we knew next to nothing about white­tails. I worked as post forester and wildlife biologist for the U.S. Military Academy at West Point for eight years in the late ’60s and early ’70s, and one of my jobs was to manage the hunting program on the academy’s 16,000 acres in southern New York. I recall seeing large scratch marks under trees where some animal had pawed away leaves, but I had no clue what had done it or why. And neither did any­one else I talked to.

Industry observers note that then came new research as modern wildlife man­agement started to steamroll along, and we learned that those pawed areas were spots that somehow were linked to whitetail bucks before and during the rut. Now we call those disturbed areas “scrapes,” as every whitetail hunter from age 8 to 80 knows. Along with the research came the inevitable desire to “improve” whitetails and grow bucks with bigger and bigger racks. Studies on nutrition and genetics unearthed the means to grow super bucks. Intensive management was suddenly the name of the game around the country. People devel­oped genetically altered monster bucks, put up fences to contain them and began to sell their semen for about as much as my pickup truck cost. Since then breeding has become big business. And in some circles, hunting has become a matter of horn inches rather than the experience itself.

In a recent development, am I complaining? Not at all. In fact, some good pals of mine run commercial whitetail preserves where intense management produces massive racks for their clients. That’s their business. And it’s here to stay. I simply see it as a sad commentary when we focus on the size of the rack rather than the smells, sights, and sounds of a damp oak forest and the raucous cries of jays and crows. Everything in the woods contributes to the total experience — and if a spike or forkhorn buck shows up, then you can be proud to flip off the safety, squeeze the trigger and smile all the way home.

Industry observers note that happily, this big-buck syn­drome hasn’t affected everyone yet. Plenty of hunters, young and old, are still thrilled to down a forkhorn buck, but new management concepts threaten the option of taking younger bucks. Biologically speaking, it’s indeed smart to let the younger bucks in some habitats live another year or two. My problem with the new techniques is that we continue to focus on the size of the antlers.

Proponents of associations that pro­mote minimum antler restrictions steadfastly insist they aren’t focusing on trophy deer. But it seems to me that when you require a deer to be of a cer­tain size before you can shoot it, it’s trophy hunting, pure and simple. Yes, these techniques work in some areas; it just bothers me that we are forced to adhere to those rules. Call me old­fashioned if you like, but I hanker for the good old days.

Read Next: Why Do I Hunt? The Answer to Hunting’s Toughest Question.

It has been revealed that I wrote about this subject recently and a reader wrote back and called me a hypocrite. He remarked that I write for OUTDOOR LIFE and that this magazine endorses trophy-buck hunt­ing. Well, hellooooo. Show me a hunting magazine that doesn’t promote big-buck hunting. There aren’t any. Show me a magazine with a forkhorn buck on the cover. There might have been one, once, but I never saw it.

In a recent development, it’s human nature to appreciate qual­ity. That’s why the Guinness Book of World Records and the Miss America pageant have such appeal. We admire the biggest, the best.

A hunter who gets a truly big buck, even when it’s total luck, becomes an instant hero. He endorses products, appears in ads, gives seminars and is a big name in hunting circles. The vast majority of these trophy owners just happened to be at the right place at the right time. Most did not “pattern” the buck, watching it for months before the season and discovering what trails it used. The lucky person was simply in the correct tree stand when the buck happened to walk by.

In a recent development, whitetail hunting today is totally for­eign to what it was when I killed my first buck. In much of the country, farm­ing practices and more restrictive hunt­ing produces older bucks with larger antlers. High fences and nutritional supplements aren’t necessary in those places. Pals who live in the Midwest, for example, say that a few decades ago they never saw the likes of the bucks running around now. I’ve been hunting Iowa for years. The size of the bucks showing up these days is scary.

All of us would like to shoot a substantial buck, myself included. Personally, I have a problem with antlers. When I see them, as long as they’re legal, the rifle is likely to swing up to my shoulder. There are exceptions, such as on a recent hunt in Kansas where I was told all sorts of 150-class bucks were waltzing around. I never saw one. I passed on plenty of other dandy bucks, ended up never firing a shot and cussed myself all the way home. Then there was the time in Saskatchewan, when a buck scoring 162 walked under my stand. It was pure dumb luck. I shot him, and I’m proud of him, and he’s my biggest buck ever, but I’m even more proud of a little six­pointer that hangs next to him.

But that’s another story. As they say, a trophy is in the eye of the beholder. That’s the bottom line.

No-Oxygen Team Will Try Again on Everest

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (377 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest.
  • “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • Sources indicate that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is promptly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

“We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

Sources indicate that in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

According to recent reports, on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

Once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

Today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.
