#91280. From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4049 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

From Icy Morning to Dead Phone — John Muir Trail Day 22

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass.
  • According to recent reports, probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm!
  • But had it been just a little colder, I would have been overwhelmed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  48,865 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  22:07.

The night before I dropped down steeply from Donohue Pass. In addition to the extra mileage, I also figured it would be warmer at that lower elevation. The camping spot I selected, looking out at a huge golden, grassy meadow, was lovely.

According to recent reports, probably it was warmer there, but that did not mean it was warm! It was already chilly when I went to sleep, and as the night went on it just got colder and colder. I gradually added items to my sleeping bag — sleeping bag liner, long pants, long shirt, puffy hat, gloves — until I used up the entirety of my anti-cold arsenal.

Fortunately, that did the trick. But had it been just a little colder, I would have been overwhelmed. It created a cognitive conflict during my pee errands in the night. My temperature sensors urged me to return to the tent as rapidly as possible. My spiritual-aesthetic soul urged me to spend just a little more time under the glorious blanket of moon and stars.

Towards morning, I had a bizarre dream. It this alternate reality, I was having a hot affair with a woman. Actually, it was a cold affair. Why? Because she was really an alien, part of an extraterrestrial race that was thinking of settling on earth, but who didn’t like our climate. It was too hot for them. Having superior technology, however, they were able to manipulate Earth climate and make it much colder to their liking. So, I was freezing cold, despite having this torrid affair.

According to recent reports, another capability of the alien was that she could make you mostly forget what you had done the night before. So, I kind of knew I was having the affair, but also wasn’t completely sure that I was. The hilarious part was that the alien in the dream was my wife’s friend DG from middle school! When I told Lee about the dream, I had to swear that I had never, ever contemplated having an affair with DG!

Did this moonlight view up through the tent inspire my strange dream?

Recent findings suggest that when it began to get light, I gave myself a little bit of a break because it had been so cold. My last trip outside the tent in the early dawn I looked out on that golden meadow and saw that it was all white, coated with icy rime.

By the time I took this picture, the rime was already melting, but some is still visible.

I also retrieved my bear cannister; it too had a layer of ice on the top cover.

In close-up, the ice on the bear cannister is very visible.

In a recent development, by this I knew it had gone below freezing during the night. So, I allowed myself some extra minutes of warmth in the sleeping bag while I waited for the sun to rise above the lip of the mountains.

I finally got up at 6:30. When the sun came up the temperature rose rapidly, but the problem then was that the ice on my tent fly became moisture. Also, the floor was pitched on a sort of pine needle-covered mud. This was very comfortable, but it ended up sticking to my ground sheet. It took some time and effort to get everything dry and clean.

It has been revealed that after all the morning errands, I did not get on the road until – wait for it – ten a.m.! On a short day, that might not have mattered, but I was planning another 17+ miles for this day. The good news was, that I was camped in the Lyell Valley, and the mostly flat trail followed the Lyell Fork river for almost nine miles, all the way to Tuolumne Meadows.

Sometimes the river and trail were close like this, sometimes farther apart.

With this cruisy route (and my late departure) I turned on the jets as I headed out. With my unfortunate record of falling on easy trails, I was also trying to be careful.

Hard to get lost on this trail!

A good portion of the trail, especially in the meadows, was indented into the earth. My feet were below the ground level in a narrow track. In this configuration, I find that hiking poles are more hazard than help. So, for most of the first nine miles, I was carrying my poles rather than using them.

In a recent development, the statistics tell the tale. Over those nine miles, I was only over 20 minutes (3 mph) twice. My best mile I did in 17:49. That is no record speed, but I don’t think I was even close to that pace anywhere else on the trail.

The scenery was interesting, but not spectacular. The main thing, with this wide-open valley, was that I could measure my progress visually. I could see an unusual-shaped mountain lining the valley up ahead; then after a time it was closer; then I was opposite to it; and then it was starting to fall behind me. In a slower progression, I could see the distant mountains at the foot of the valley ahead (where the river changes direction). At first, they were far distant, then middle distant, and eventually they were quite close.

The wide glacial valley, filled with meadows, and the mountains at the far end that grew larger as I got closer.

Sources indicate that at faster than 3 mph, I was in Tuolumne Meadows in under three hours. As I got closer it was apparent there was a tourist center nearby. Suddenly many more persons were on the trail and most of them were geared out for just a day of hiking or fishing.

It has been revealed that the design of Tuolumne was a little weird, with a “downtown” road (Tioga Road) on the north side of the river and a hiking trail parallel on the south side. I generally don’t love road-walking. However, because the Wilderness Center (for permits) was in the middle of downtown, and because I wanted a permit to climb Half Dome the next day, I intended to go via the road.

NPS map of Tuolumne Meadows (in the lower right, I should have turned onto the “National Scenic Trail” but instead stayed on the John Muir Trail).

It has been revealed that I missed the turn. Maybe my feet just wanted to stay in the woods? As I realized my error, I ran into a really nice couple who were staying at the fancy lodge nearby. They had a map, and they confirmed, “Yeah, you just have to go back to that last turn and then turn to go across the river, instead of going straight.”.

According to recent reports, I had a sudden aversion to that initiative, particularly because of the miles I wanted to hike that day. The woman must have seen my expression, because she said, “My husband is just like you; he hates to backtrack!”.

Industry observers note that it was true. So, I noted, “Maybe I’ll go to the Visitor Center instead, and they can help me there.”  I continued on.

Sources indicate that now I was surrounded by roads and parking lots. As I passed one lot, I saw a uniformed ranger manning the booth and I walked up to him. When I explained what I wanted, he said, “First of all, to get a permit, you have to go to the Wilderness Center. Second, they will not give you a permit to climb Half Dome. The only way to get a Half Dome permit is to get a whole different multi-day permit that includes climbing Half Dome within it.”.

Now that had not been my understanding, but he seemed very confident. At this point I was even further away from the Wilderness Center and even less inclined to backtrack. I could see my Half Dome ambitions evaporating. I figured I could still go to the Visitor Center and give it one last try.

It has been revealed that en route I saw that I would pass the market that hosted the famous Tuolumne Grill, and I realized that it was just about lunchtime. I left my pack outside and went in to order. It seemed a simple layout with some picnic tables outside to eat what you ordered. I got a regular hamburger that came with orange juice and some wedge potatoes. The juice tasted delicious on this now-hot day, and the wedges, slathered with ketchup, were good too. But the hamburger? It was an ordinary sort of dry hockey puck, not terrible, but not special at all. I concluded the Grill was famous because of where it was, and not for what it served.

In a recent development, as I ate it all, I took my phone off of Airplane Mode and called my wife, Lee. (I always hike with it in Airplane Mode to preserve my battery charge.)  When I told her the likely new proposal, without Half Dome, she sounded excited that I was almost done. I was looking forward to seeing her soon as well.

The Visitor Center was a mile-long road walk from there. I had two animal encounters (of a sort) along the way.

First, I saw wild turkeys! How funny to spend all that time in the wilderness without seeing any (though I did see grouse). Then in congested Tuolumne I saw them. I even got some pictures.

If not for the legs, the turkey blended in….

Second, as I was walking, a car slowed way down opposite me and the driver shouted out his window, “A bear just walked across the road up ahead less than five minutes ago!”.

Sources indicate that I shouted back, “Good! I hope I see him, because I am getting really hungry!”.

Recent findings suggest that whether he was pulling my leg, or he really saw the bear, I did not see any bear. I was definitely looking out for it though.

After pine forest and silence, it was disconcerting to walk on asphalt with diesel engines roaring past me. I was glad it was only a mile. On arrival, I went up to the very nice woman in front of the Visitor Center and asked about permits. No surprise, she directed me to the Wilderness Center. I concluded the fates did not intend me to climb Half Dome.

Then I asked about getting out of Yosemite when I reached Happy Isles. She explained about the free shuttle within the park that could get me to Curry Village from Happy Isles if I didn’t want to walk there. From Curry Village, the YARTS (Yosemite Area Regional Transportation System) could transport me for a fee. The end of their line was Merced, about three hours away. I figured I could take a train or bus from Merced, or maybe Gabriel could come from Santa Rosa and pick me up there.

This lady pointed to the YARTS timetable on their bulletin board and suggested I take a picture of it. I replied, “That’s a great idea! You’re a lot smarter than I am to think of it!”.

She also gave me a paper map of the Yosemite Valley to include Happy Isles and Curry Village, saying, “I know you hikers don’t like to add weight, but I think you might find this useful.”.

I told her I was sure I would and stashed it away.

Sources indicate that with that, I aimed for the trail, which passed a ways behind the Visitor Center. It was a relief to be walking on pine needles again!

It is funny how quickly the crowds taper off as you get even a short distance away from the tourist centers.

It has been revealed that the other significant change was in elevation profile. In the morning, the trail had ranged from flat to slightly downhill. Now I would face climbing up past Cathedral Lakes to Cathedral Pass. This was the last pass on the John Muir Trail. It was about 9,700 feet which was a lot lower than the passes in the south, but still more than 1,000 feet above Tuolumne Meadows.

According to recent reports, perhaps it was my energy expenditure in the morning, but now I was puffing and panting as I ascended. “Where is my juice?” I asked myself. “This is as bad as climbing Cottonwood Pass on the first day of the JMT!”.

I was breathing hard, but enjoying the enormous granite rock.

The inspiration was the views. There was more than one rocky shape that could qualify as a “cathedral.”  Imagine Notre Dame. Imagine that the roof is one thousand feet high, the spires soar over 1,500 feet, and the nave stretch two miles. Then imagine a landscape dotted with two or three of these behemoths. It was magical.

Industry observers note that about the time my legs finally got warmed up, I came across a couple that were on the first day of their John Muir Trail hike. The reversal I had imagined, when encountering near-finishers at the start of my own hike, was coming true. In chatting, he warned me, “Oh, there’s no water except at Upper Cathedral.”.

I appreciated that intel and was on the lookout for a spot near Upper Cathedral Creek. As I ascended, coming above the tree line, I was surprised not to find it. Then, as I passed a quarter mile from Upper Cathedral Lake, I saw some people emerge on a trail from the lake onto the main trail. Suddenly it dawned on me that there was no creek. He meant the lake!

Industry observers note that it was late afternoon and I wanted to press on and find a campsite. But if this was really “last water” it would be foolish not to take the detour for it.

The lake seemed to have mostly marshy and muddy access points. These would entail wet feet and dirty water to filter. However, I saw a rocky promontory jutting into the lake where a bunch of guys were hanging out. I headed there to refill my water.

According to recent reports, I began chatting with them and learned they were from Kansas City. I asked them whether they lived in Kansas or Missouri and they noted that only someone who knows Kansas City would ask that question. I explained that I had a cousin who lived in K.C. and they told me they lived on the Kansas side.

Sources indicate that overall, they were nice enough, but the banter occasionally felt a little mocking. For example, they asked me, “Did you go up Whitney?”   I replied that I had, but that I had been fighting a respiratory infection, making it very difficult.

According to recent reports, they responded, “Oh, that just adds to your story about climbing Mount Whitney. Like, ‘everybody else just climbed it, but I climbed it with a respiratory infection, coughing every step of the way!’”.

They were actually not wrong, but the tone felt a little snarky.

In a recent development, after I filled both my water bottles and my Katadyn BeFree to have maximum water available, I headed back toward the trail. One of the guys, maybe the leader, followed me a short distance and called me over. He was asking me about the trail, and it turned out he had done the trail himself a few years before. It seemed a little odd, but I took him as just wanting to reminisce a bit about his own experience.

Industry observers note that in a quarter mile I was back at the junction with the JMT. The beauty of the scenery around Cathedral Lakes is so inspiring, I wanted to take some more pictures. John Muir himself said, on summiting Cathedral Peak, “This I may say is the first time I have been at church in California, led here at last, every door graciously opened for the poor lonely worshiper.”  (Quoted from My First Summer in the Sierra, Chapter 10, entry for September 7, 1869.).

It has been revealed that so, this “lonely worshiper” reached for his smart phone to capture the majestic giants and discovered… nothing. Nothing at all, a black screen. Now my eyesight is not great without glasses, but I had thought my phone showed 65% of charge when last I checked.

Sources indicate that in case it had just shut off for some reason, I tried to restart it, but still nothing. I was crestfallen, thinking, “Oh no! My phone died here on the trail with barely one day left on my hike!!!”.

Recent findings suggest that I could not fathom how it happened. I had not dropped it that I could recall. Deeply disappointed, I began having paranoid thoughts. “If I had charge, and now suddenly I don’t, could that guy who followed me, to talk to me, have had some technology that fried my phone? Like some super magnet or something?”.

It seemed wildly implausible, but the coincidence – that it happened right after our exchange – seemed strange.

Recent findings suggest that then I calmed down somewhat. I reminded myself of what was truly crucial,  “This trip is about the experience itself. It is not ultimately about telling the story or capturing the pictures, it is about your lived experience.”.

Recent findings suggest that seen through that prism my loss was minor and I settled down. My wife and I always try to distinguish “disappointments” from “tragedies,” and this was clearly the former.

According to recent reports, with the light turning to a mellow glow in the sky, I continued hiking. Cathedral Pass was not much further. It was unusual, in that the trail reached the pass, but did not descend from there down the other side. Instead, it continued on, ascending further up the ridge of one of the mountainsides bordering the pass.

According to recent reports, now my lack of a phone was frustrating because I had lost my navigation device. I was not sure how far I should ideally go before selecting a camp, remembering that I wanted to make miles to ensure I could finish on the following day.

Recent findings suggest that the mountains answered that question for me. As I continued higher, I came to a turn on the outstretched flank of the range. Extending from the trail was a large flat spot, with visibility in all directions. The ground was ideal for pitching a tent. The views were magical in the waning light. I thought, “I can go further, and shorten my day tomorrow. Or I can camp tonight in the most beautiful spot in the Sierras.”  That decision was an easy one.

In a recent development, in Tuolumne I heard we were in for another icy night, and I was now at a higher elevation than I had been the night before. So, I was expecting cold. In fact, as the sun dropped behind the peaks, I could feel the chill almost immediately.

I started to pitch my tent, and maybe I was in too much of a hurry? I love my Significant Agnes TigerWall, but on this night, as I tried to get a pole into the slot, the pole snapped. After the dead phone, this might have been a devastating blow. But in this stunning location, on the last night I needed a tent, it did not phase me. Besides, I had been carrying a seemingly useless stupid little tube for miles and miles, wondering why I bothered, and now I had my answer. I slid the tube over the broken spot, taped it in place with surgical tape (though that might have been unnecessary), and reseated the pole in the slot. Good as latest? Maybe not, but close enough.

Having pitched my tent, I just basked in the beauty of the location for a few minutes. Then I soaked my food and found a spot for a cat hole and dug what was likely to be my last cat hole on the trail. The cold soak did not take long, but the result was the opposite of the previous night’s dinner. That food had not rehydrated fully but was wonderfully seasoned and tasted delicious. This night the mashed potatoes and chicken hydrated easily, but they were totally bland. They didn’t taste bad really, they just didn’t taste like anything at all!

Of course, mindful as always that this is fuel first and flavor second, I wolfed it all down.

According to recent reports, with no phone, I was communicating with my family by Garmin. That was so onerous, typing out everything, one letter at a time. (On the trail I learned of an app that makes this easier, but I didn’t have either the app or a working phone.)  Gabriel seemed amenable to picking me up in Merced, and so I realized I needed to make massive speed the next day to get to Happy Isles. The 4:50 p.m. YARTS departure to Merced arrived by 8:30 p.m. Even that would mean getting back to Santa Rosa by midnight, after all. Our back and forth about this on the Garmin was practically in code, but I thought the initiative was set.

It has been revealed that wrapping up my chores in deep twilight, I stored everything in my bear cannister and – why not? — I hooked my phone to the charger.

Before going to sleep, I decided to just take a peek at the phone. What?? Yes! Yes!! My phone was charging!!!

In a recent development, I was elated and still baffled as to how it happened. I could not be sure. The best explanation I came up with was this:  First, without my glasses I had misread the charge level on the phone. It did not have 65%, it must have had much less. Second, after speaking with my wife from the restaurant at lunch, I must not have turned Airplane Mode back on, so that the phone drained far more rapidly in the afternoon than it did in the morning. That is my best guess. Operator error.

The most beautiful campsite — taken under the stars, after my phone revived.

Snuggled in my tent, I got gussied up, wearing all of my clothing in preparation for a second icy cold night.

My tent in the moonlight of the last night — repaired and welcoming (except for the mess inside!).

It boggled my mind to think that – most probably – I was wrapped in my sleeping bag for the last time this year. The excitement of (hopefully) completing the trail the next day would normally have kept me wide awake. But no. I was just too tired and slept right away.

Kilimanjaro, to name a few. It was my honor to serve my country as a diplomat around the world for 34 years. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • Recent findings suggest that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

Recent findings suggest that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Industry observers note that eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

The Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

#91274. How to Soap-Tan a Rabbit Hide at Home

How to Soap-Tan a Rabbit Hide at Home

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that during the cold winter months, rabbit hunting is one of my favorite things to do.
  • Rabbit fur is incredibly soft and beautiful when it’s prime, and at the beginning of rabbit season this year I decided to start saving my rabbit hides to eventually make a blanket.
  • I knew that it would take quite a few rabbit pelts to create a blanket for anyone other than a baby, and sending them away to be professionally tanned would cost more than I wanted to spend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that during the cold winter months, rabbit hunting is one of my favorite things to do. Especially right after a fresh snow—there’s nothing like flinging arrows at cottontails.

Rabbit fur is incredibly soft and beautiful when it’s prime, and at the beginning of rabbit season this year I decided to start saving my rabbit hides to eventually make a blanket.

I knew that it would take quite a few rabbit pelts to create a blanket for anyone other than a baby, and sending them away to be professionally tanned would cost more than I wanted to spend. So, I decided to tan the rabbit hides on my own.

I have tanned several deer hides, squirrels, fox, coyote, and mink. Rabbit, however, is a completely different story. If you’ve ever skinned a cottontail rabbit, you’ll know that their hides are the “tissue paper” of furbearing animals. Their skin is so thin and delicate that you can easily skin them without using a knife.

Sources indicate that there are many ways to tan animal hides, and it can be overwhelming. Even once you decide on a specific method, there are various ways to approach it. After several nights of scouring the internet, including many taxidermy sites, I discovered a method called soap tanning that looked like it might work for rabbits. All the instructions I found were vague, but the process seemed simple enough. Not only does this method use simple household items, but it’s free of harsh chemicals. That means it’s safe to do indoors, and with small children and animals around.

Related: How to Butcher a Rabbit.

Sources indicate that the whole process, excluding the drying, only took me about an hour from start to finish. It was very simple, and the hide came out beautifully. So, don’t toss those bunny furs next time you bag a few—save and tan them! You can tan the hides fresh, or put them in a Ziploc bag and freeze them until you’re ready to start the process. Thaw 24 hours prior to tanning.

Recent findings suggest that the first step is probably the most difficult step because, as I noted above, rabbit hide is very thin and tears easily. Most hides are fleshed with a fleshing tool, but that doesn’t work for rabbit hides as it would destroy the thin skin. Working slowly is the best way to avoid tears, but if you do end up tearing the hide, it can be fixed later.

Sources indicate that place the hide fur-side down, flesh-side up on your board. Using the tacks (or nails, like I did) pin the rabbit hide to the board. You’ll want the hide to be taut, but don’t try to stretch it too much. Your hide may be an odd shape, but that’s okay. That will be fixed later, and it’s better to leave it oddly shaped for now.

Recent findings suggest that once the hide is in place, use the flat side of a butter knife to gently scrape up the layer of flesh from the hide. The flesh will be slightly pink, and the hide underneath will be black and white. Hold the knife horizontal, keeping it as parallel to the hide as much as possible.

Recent findings suggest that once you’ve scraped enough away, you can grab the flesh with your hands and slowly peel it back from the hide, a little at a time to prevent tearing. Once you do this a few times, this goes fairly quickly. Be extra careful around holes in the hide that have been left behind from bullets or broadheads.

Once all the flesh has been peeled from the hide, remove the nails from the hide, and remove the hide from the board.

It has been revealed that place the hide in a clean bowl or bucket, and add a cup of olive oil. The measurement isn’t really important; just add enough to saturate the hide. Using your hands, work the oil into the skin side (not the hair) until you see the skin start to turn translucent. Don’t worry if you get oil on the hair side, though, since you’ll wash it in the next step.

In another clean bowl or bucket, add enough room temperature water to submerge the hide completely.

According to recent reports, add a healthy dose of dish soap (I used roughly half of a bottle). Again, measurements aren’t extremely key, you just want a strong ratio of soap to water.

It has been revealed that using a large wooden spoon or your hands, gently stir the hide in the soap and water. I started with a spoon and found it easier to use my hands. Be careful not to stir too vigorously, as this will make any holes in the hide even bigger.

Industry observers note that keep stirring the hide until the skin side starts turning white. Once all areas have gone from translucent to white, you’re going to test a small piece.

Do this by bringing a small pot of water to a boil. Trim a small piece of the rabbit hide that’s roughly 2- x ½-inch. (This is a great way to use a ragged edge that you want to trim off to fix the shape.).

Recent findings suggest that drop it into the pot of boiling water and leave it for approximately 30 seconds. Then use tongs to remove the hide and let it rest on a towel for a second. If the hide curls and is stiff, add more soap to your soap and water solution, and continue stirring. If the hide comes out of the boiling water and is still soft and pliable, your soap tan is complete.

Take your hide out of the soap and water solution, and run it under room-temperature water until all the soap is gone. Gently squeeze the hide to remove as much excess water as possible.

In a recent development, at this point, you’ll be able to trim the edges of your hide if you so choose. You’ll also want to sew any holes in the hide.

Cut a piece of thread about a foot long. Make a small knot in the one end of your thread, and thread the opposite end through your needle. You’ll want to use a simple whip stitch on the skin side to close the holes. Keep your stitches snug, but not so tight that the skin puckers. The edges of the hole should touch, but not overlap. This will result in smooth fur on the opposite side, with no lumps and bumps.

It has been revealed that this is the longest part of the process. It took roughly 24 hours for the rabbit hide to dry completely. You’ll want to keep it in a dry area, away from pets and make sure no mice or rodents can get to it.

Recent findings suggest that hanging it on a hook or draping it over a rack so air can get to both the skin and fur side will ensure even drying. The hide will probably shrink a bit as it dries, but this is normal.

Recent findings suggest that you can soften the hide during the drying process, or after. Trying to stretch a rabbit hide just rips it in half, so simply folding it and rolling it into a ball is the easiest way to soften the hide and make it more supple. If you skip this step, however, your hide will still be extremely easy to work with if you are going to use it for a sewing project.

According to recent reports, the final step to tanning many hides is to smoke the hide over smoldering coals. Wet hides tend to dry stiff, even if they’ve been worked really well, and the smoke essentially “finishes” the hide in case it were ever to get water on it.

Industry observers note that I chose to skip this step, as I strategy on making a blanket once I have enough pelts, and it’s fairly unlikely that the blanket will ever get wet. On top of that, rabbit hides are so thin that even if they were to stiffen, they would still be very pliable.

If you do choose to smoke your rabbit hide, it only takes about 30 minutes. Keep in mind that smoking will change the color of the hide.

Read Next: Hunting Rabbits is the Perfect Cure for Winter Cabin Fever.

Decide what you want to do with the hide. The possibilities are endless, whether you choose to display the hide on an end table, create fur trim on a garment, or save a dozen to create a pillow or blanket.

#91271. Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3130 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3130 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures.
  • Sources indicate that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet.
  • Whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures. And as strange as it may sound, bass and deer are really very much alike, at least in the ways they respond to bitter cold weather.

Sources indicate that wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet. However, bass do begin exhibiting changed behavior. Generally bass will drift away from the shallows and into deeper water as the thermometer falls because temperatures in the depths remain relatively stable on a day-to-day basis. Here, their metabolisms begin to wind down. The bass, therefore, do not require as much food intake to sustain various bodily functions. Consequently, these two alterations in their lifestyle can make them very tough to catch for all but the most experienced fishermen.

Whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself. Yet few people, aside from biologists, are aware that deer also eat less as extremely cold weather approaches. Chemical changes take place in their bodies, causing their digestive processes to switch to s-l-o-w. This, in turn, allows for the maintenance of various body systems at a greatly reduced rate of food intake.

Another important point to emphasize about the anatomies of whitetails is that their brains are comparatively small in relation to their overall body sizes. Therefore, the integrated nervous system coursing throughout their bodies is rudimentary at best. As a result, like most wild creatures that do not possess a sophisticated neural apparatus, their pain thresholds are quite high — making them relatively insensitive to bitter cold temperatures. Many hunters are not aware of this because for generations they’ve been led to believe that when the weather goes sour, deer can be expected to do this or that in order “to seek protection from the elements and be more comfortable.”.

Body comfort actually has little to do with their changed behavior patterns. After all, the northern boundary of the whitetail’s native range extends more than 150 miles beyond the United States/Canadian border to approximately 52° latitude. Anyone who has lived thereabouts can tell you that winter temperatures frequently average -20°. The wind-chill factor often makes it seem as cold as -75°. Therefore, it just doesn’t stand to reason that animal species such as whitetails would be native to such hostile climes were they not virtually immune to such weather.

We’ve even seen evidence of this immunity right on our southern-Ohio farm where it is not uncommon to experience at least several days of -20° temperatures each winter.

Behind my barn there is an old tractor trail that wends its way through a 40-acre oak forest. Numerous times, while hauling out firewood, I’ve seen deer bedded on nearby slopes. Often they reveal a thick dusting of newly introduced-fallen snow covering their backs — the hollow hairs of their coats providing such superb insulation that their body heat is unable to escape. If I approach too closely, the deer will predictably rise to their feet, shake themselves like soaking-wet dogs and cause clouds of snowflakes to fly — then saunter off to other parts with an air of nonchalance at having been rousted from their beds.

If deer are able to adapt to such gelid temperatures so easily, why is it then, that legions of otherwise knowledgeable hardworking hunters so often strike out when the freeze is on?

Industry observers note that say, for example, that you’ve been hunting in balmy temperatures for several days, have had the opportunity to look over a number of animals but haven’t seen anything you’d really be satisfied with. So you’ve decided to hold out a while longer, hoping you’ll eventually stumble onto “Mr. Significant.”.

Recent findings suggest that suddenly, you wake up one morning to the sound of icy sleet pinging against your bedroom window. Bounding from the rack, you are shocked to discover that the wind is whistling a siren song and that overnight the temperature has dropped 35°.

After sitting on a stand for several hours that morning without seeing a thing, you look and feel like a popsicle. So you begin moving around — sneak hunting — but eventually conclude that the deer have vanished. By day’s end the temperature has fallen another 10°, a light skiff of hoarfrost blankets the ground and your expectations have long since dwindled. You’ve forgotten entirely about taking a nice buck this season and have begun thinking that if you can just manage to fill your doe tag you’ll be very very lucky.

According to recent reports, the scenario is the bane of all hunters living north of the Mason-Dixon Line. Because it’s obvious that the deer couldn’t possibly have just disappeared from the face of the earth, the best prospect for success undoubtedly lies in learning more about their behavioral reactions to severe weather.

According to recent reports, one of the most telling clues to unraveling the mystery of their disappearance can be traced to changes in the whitetails’ body chemistry — the changes that cause them to require less food. Biologists say that this is an annual occurrence and that, like the rut, it is triggered by progressively shorter days and diminished periods of sunlight. Sometime around mid-November, the growth hormone thyroxin, which for the past eight months has been flooding the body, begins dissipating and will remain at a very low level until the following spring.

According to recent reports, this shoots down another popular myth about bucks not feeding much during the rut because they are so love struck. Actually, their reduced food intake can be attributed to a conservation measure on the part of nature. In other words, with each additional week of cold weather, food becomes less and less available so nature accordingly reduces the animals’ need for food by enacting significant changes in their body metabolisms.

Industry observers note that hunters should realize that, as the season progresses and as increasing numbers of severe polar blasts begin descending upon their regions, deer can be expected to move around less and less in search of food. The movements they do exhibit are no longer going to be concentrated during the traditional early and late hours of the day but during midday when it is likely to be warmer. Again, the deer are not seeking “comfort” but rather are conserving energy to more efficiently make use of the sharply reduced food supplies.

It has been revealed that I’ve seen this happen with such consistency that I now almost consider it axiomatic. At our northern-Minnesota hunting camp, for example, members of our regular group begin bowhunting in October. We’ve learned from more than 80 years of combined experience that the odds of taking a whitetail early in the season are in our favor if we take up early-morning stands, nap during midday when deer are bedded, then resume our vigils late in the afternoon.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant.

Yet during the final days of the gun season in December, those in our party who still have not scored have entirely reversed their strategies. Now the order of the day, paradoxically perhaps, is to sleep late in the morning, wait on stand during midday, then quit early. There’s just not enough likelihood of seeing anything move — particularly at dawn’s first light — to justify the oftentimes agonizing ordeal of sitting as still as a statue in weather so bitter cold that it gnaws at your innermost fiber.

Industry observers note that of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant. As far as they’re concerned, they want to be in the field every available minute. That’s fine and dandy but, if they want to maximize their chances for success, they should still be willing to make certain adjustments in the way they hunt.

Industry observers note that late in the season, and particularly when the freeze is on, they should stillhunt or sneak hunt early and late in the day when deer are most likely to be sequestered in their beds. During midday, hunters should play the waiting game on stand when deer are inclined to be traveling to and from feeding sites.

But where, exactly, do the deer go when the bottom falls out of the thermometer and ice storms or sheets of wind-driven sleet are lashing the countryside? The three-pronged answer to this is thick cover on a protected south-facing slope in a low-elevation area of terrain.

In a recent development, two of the most desirable types of thick cover are dense stands of head-high honeysuckle and nearly impenetrable pine plantations. The pines are most often thickets of immature trees that have their whorls of branches close to the ground.

In the face of adverse weather, deer retreat deep into such seclusions where they can wait out the ensuing tempest. Again, trying to stay warm or achieve some other comfort level has little to do with their evasive behavior. Windy stormy weather makes whitetails extremely restless and nervous. By their very nature, whitetails are already hypertensive and are extremely paranoid creatures. When they’re no longer able to detect, classify and catalog sounds and scents because of the competition from noisy winds and erratic air currents, they waste no time finding a place where they can maintain a low profile. Therefore, rather than allowing themselves to remain vulnerable by bedding on their customary hillside benches and ridgelines, they retreat into deep thick cover. This not only helps to block the wind but perhaps also gives them the feeling that hiding from ready view somewhat compensates for their impaired senses.

Sources indicate that once, for a period of several days in the dead of winter, I had the opportunity to watch an eight-point whitetail buck in a fenced enclosure. This was a wild deer that had recently been captured by biologists for use in various nutrition studies. Its temporary fenced-in home was five acres of relatively open hardwood forest with scattered swatches of second-growth ground cover here and there.

Industry observers note that whenever the weather was warm, sunny and there was no wind, the buck had a particular place it liked to bed. The deer could see in every direction from the high hammock. Yet whenever a frontal storm system moved through the region and the wind began howling, the deer promptly vacated its usual turf. It always went downhill into a little pocket of thick multiflora rose — the only significant cover in the compound — and buried itself right in the middle.

One day as snow clouds scudded against an ominously gray sky and ice-riddled branches creaked in the wind, I watched in amazement as the buck laid on his belly for long hours, his front legs outstretched and his chin resting on the ground. Yet when the wind occasionally intensified with its typical freight-train drone, or an ice-laden branch suddenly crashed to the ground, the buck’s head would instantly come up, swiveling in all directions. Assured that nothing was on the prowl, the buck would then quickly duck back down again. Moments later his head would be up, down, then back up again. Just observing all that nervous energy and pent-up anxiety exhausted me — under these conditions the buck’s entire personality was like a violin string about to snap.

I’m confident that the penned buck would have liked to have had access to much thicker deeper cover to increase his feeling of security. I’m also certain that unconfined deer in their native habitat behave much the same way when the freeze is on. Moreover, a biologist at the research station told me that during one terrible winter storm, the penned buck stayed put for four consecutive days until the weather finally abated.

In addition to tangled jungles of honeysuckle and conifer forests, whitetails also like to retreat into swamps when the freeze is on. Because of the continually decaying organic matter, swamps are always warmer than other regions and this, coupled with the fact that they’re always found in low-lying terrain, keeps them somewhat sheltered from the brunt of the weather.

However, without meaning to again kick the proverbial dead horse, deer don’t seek out swamps in order to stay warm. They go there because past experience has taught them that they’re not likely to bump into hunters in such forbidding territory and, similarly, a swamp is one place where they can continue to effectively rely upon their senses to forewarn them of impending danger.

Yet no matter what type of cover deer may elect to use for hiding, hunting them when the freeze is on can be extremely difficult because the animals’ minds and senses are so preoccupied with monitoring their immediate surroundings. But there are several tactics that seem to be far more productive than others.

First, of course, pay attention to weather forecasts. Deer seem to have built-in barometers that give them advance notice when hostile weather is about to assault their regions. They take due advantage of this insight by stocking up on groceries, instinctively knowing that once the bitter weather strikes it will preclude safe traveling to and from feeding sites for several days. Then, immediately after the frontal system has passed and calmness again prevails, the deer come out of hiding and return to their favorite food plots. Consequently, stand hunting or sneak hunting — just before and immediately after a storm — are two key strategies no enterprising whitetail hunter can afford to pass up.

Cornfields can be prime places to try because, throughout the Midwest and the northern border states, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing as long as possible. In the past, it was either chopped or combined sometime in October or November. But with storage costs escalating like never before and future market prices uncertain, many farmers nowadays are leaving the corn in the field until such time as they have a specific need for it or until the price increases. Quite often this means as late as February.

Already-picked cornfields are also good bets because a substantial amount of harvest residue may continue to draw deer months after the corn has been combined. On our own cornfields we’re sometimes amazed to see a dozen deer at a time pawing through a foot of snow cover to find spillage.

I emphasize the importance of finding corn when the freeze is on because native wild foods are becoming more and more sparse with each additional week of winter weather. Other popular agricultural foods such as soybeans are rarely allowed to remain in the field beyond their peak harvest times, so corn is a deer magnet beyond compare.

In a recent development, hunting during a storm can also pay off. The best opportunity occurs when the temperature does not fall dramatically. This usually means that the wind velocity will not be too fierce and any precipitation is likely to be in the form of huge wet snowflakes that begin clinging to cover like giant globs of cotton candy. Under such conditions, whitetails don’t seem to become as jittery and frantic about their safety and may continue to feed during midday periods. The fluffy snow itself may also pacify them just enough during nonfeeding periods so that they will remain tied to their usual haunts rather than diving headlong into thick security cover.

Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground.

Sources indicate that conversely, hunting during the most ravaging freeze-outs offers the least chance of success. Now, patiently waiting on stand is inherently a futile endeavor. The animals simply will not come to you. It is necessary for you to go find them by prowling through swamps, honeysuckle or evergreens.

Never try to approach such cover on level ground. Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground. This will allow you to look down and through the cover and will make it far easier to spot bedded or sneaking deer.

Another option is to round up several pals and begin staging drives, particularly in the case of expansive pine plantations. Here is a unique situation, not unlike hunting rabbits, where the drivers themselves are likely to be awarded as many shots as the hunters placed on stand. The reason, as we briefly touched on earlier, is because deer that have retreated into the catacombs of thick cover are extremely reluctant to expose themselves, to travel great distances or to sever their close ties with that chosen cover where they’ve decided to holeup. As a result, a buck pushed out by a driver may chart a bounding weaving escape flight that actually takes him only a very short distance before he promptly ducks back down to resume hiding.

Read Next: Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck.

Because the drivers are likely to see a good deal of shooting, those hunters placed on stand should use portable tree stands situated as high as practical so they are not in the direct line of fire of their approaching partners. Also — and this cannot be emphasized too strongly — every hunter participating in such a maneuver should be fully clad in fluorescent orange clothing and should maintain loud voice contact so everyone is well aware of each other’s location.

When hunting during freezing stormy weather, wise garment selection also requires careful thought. For sneak hunting or stillhunting, wool is always the best bet because it is noiseless when the fabric grates against brambles and brush. But when toughing out long hours on stand, I rely exclusively upon down-filled duds and bundle up like a snowman.

In a recent development, I’d be the last to say that hunting deer when the freeze is on is purely enjoyable. Human beings just weren’t designed with bitter-cold weather in mind. But when such conditions prevail, any hunter can indeed fill his tag. Just keep in mind the changed behavior the animals are certain to begin exhibiting and blueprint your strategy accordingly.

This story was originally published in the November 1987 issue of Outdoor Life.

  • The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.
  • Sources indicate that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

Sources indicate that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

It has been revealed that “That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

This means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” mentioned Kondrashkin.

Sources indicate that the fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

It has been revealed that on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

#91268. Swatara Treasure Hunt

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Swatara Treasure Hunt

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I battle rocks and falling temperatures while searching for a lost item on trail.
  • Sources indicate that my plans are rarely flexible, until they are.
  • I texted my change in looks to Pebbles as I made my way down the trail.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I battle rocks and falling temperatures while searching for a lost item on trail.

Sources indicate that my plans are rarely flexible, until they are. I checked in with Pebbles last night to see what she, Rebar, and Greasetrap had planned (Soaked completed his hike the previous day, huge congrats to him!). They planned to slack-packing 15 miles starting from Swatara Gap and heading south. I would be doing the same – but I had the section heading north scheduled first. Not a significant deal, I could just swap them. However, my section south of Swatara Gap called for 24 miles of hiking. I would need to start early and hike flat out all day to make it before sunset. I knew that isn’t really their style, which is valid. I had made up my mind and was sticking to my initiative. I was up early and decided to head towards town to buy a coffee. While enjoying my hot beverage in my car I decided to take one last look at both itineraries. I might not be able to hike with them, but simply flipping my current section might allow me to pass them early in the day. Eventually I have to earn my trail name, right? I set a course for Swatara Gap and was on trail close to 8:00AM.

I texted my change in looks to Pebbles as I made my way down the trail. No sooner had I switched my phone into airplane mode and put it back in my pack than 3 hikers appeared ahead. Ca-caw! The group chimed. Ca-caw! I called back. Soon we were catching up and discussing our future hiking plans and Rebars new kicks. His previous Altras had taken a beating on the trail, I recall him putting some kind of indestructible adhesive on them during a previous encounter. He now had a snazzy new pair of Altras and was clearly enjoying the upgrade. After chatting for a few minutes we agreed to keep in close contact since I’ll soon be skipping ahead of them to close out my hike. The trail crosses the Swatara Creek on the 19th century Waterville Bridge, an interesting piece of industrial era engineering.

As I approached the bridge, I felt my phone vibrate. I had left it on since I had parked my car in a lot that requires calling the state park if you intend to leave your vehicle there overnight. I thought I might get a call back since I left a message. Instead I saw that it was Pebbles calling me. “So, you know how you like treasure hunts? Well, Rebar left a dry bag at the last campsite…”. For the third time, I was going to help the crew out by retrieving an object they’d left behind. I think I could make a living doing this professionally given the dozens of items reported missing on FarOut. Drive to the nearest trailhead, hike out and retrieve the item, drive it up the trail or ship it back to its owner, profit. Of course, for friends I’ll stick with the rate of a few guava candies. A few miles later I was staring at a bag resting neatly by a fire pit, it was definitely Rebar’s, my easiest find yet!

The trail had leveled off onto another long ridge, but the rocks made sure things weren’t too easy for me. The rocks and cold became the theme of the day. I had endured many cold days but not one single time had I ended a day with my sleeping layers still on. Hiking always warmed me up a ton and often after 30-minutes of hiking I’d shed them and hike in my shorts and sun hoodie. The climb out of Swatara Gap warmed me up and had me considering stopping to make the adjustment. But I wanted to see how I felt once the climbing stopped and I was just moving along the mostly level ridge. My temperature returned to a comfortable level quickly, so I was content to keep moving and keep the layers on. There were a handful of views along the ridge, but otherwise minimal points of interest aside from some boulder fields.

Classic Pennsylvania ridge rocks.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Looking south from the ridge north of Swatara Gap.

Eventually I came to Route 501. I considered taking the path to the 501 Shelter, but the comments on FarOut said it was boarded up with no facilities for hikers. That didn’t sound worth documenting for the blog so I continued along the AT a few miles to the Showers Steps viewpoint. It was a gorgeous view, but unlike many of the viewpoints from the ridges I have been hiking along it faced the sunset. It was cloudy, but there were signs that some semblance of a sunset might be visible. A few breaks in the clouds, tunnels of light illuminating small areas of the valley below. I hadn’t planned to camp here, but a check of FarOut revealed that I had just enough time to hike to Route 183 and back if I really hauled. There were more viewpoints ahead so I decided to check those out and make a decision along the way.

According to recent reports, the trail traded rocky sections with cruisy for the next few miles. Each viewpoint I passed faced too far toward the east to offer a view of the sunset. They probably would have been great for sunrise, but it was supposed to be cloudy. Sunrise would be a total question mark as to whether there would be much to see. Today’s sunset at least had a little promise. In fact, the beams of sun were occasionally shining on the trail, I felt external warmth for the first time all day. Was it a sign that I should camp at Showers Steps? I figured that was the best plan and hurried down the trail.

On my way back I stopped at the Hertlein Creek to collect water for the evening. I stopped at the first trickle of water, which meant I missed seeing the nearby campsites and swimming hole complete with rope swing. It probably wasn’t the right weather for the latter but it would have been cool to have a quick look-see.

Sources indicate that I was back at the Showers Steps in time for sunset, but I could tell the whole way back that was not really going to be much to see. The clouds had rolled back in, some quite dark. The view was still great, just not quite what I’d hustled for. I pitched my tent near a makeshift shelter, noticing that, by some miracle, my tent was already mostly dry. The rain two nights ago had soaked it, I expected a long wait for it dry out in the 40 degree weather, but was pleasantly surprised that I could go right ahead and set up my bed for the night. Soon I was bracing for the night, which was going be perhaps the coldest night I’ve spent in my tent all year.

More of Pennsylvania’s “state flower”.

Industry observers note that A memorial to William F. Shanaman near the Showers Steps.

The view from Showers Steps in the early afternoon.

A cruisy and photogenic section of the trail.

Looking west from the trail near Hertlein Creek.

Decent and collectable flow at Hertlein Creek.

Looking west from the trail near Hertlein Creek.

Looking west from the trail near Hertlein Creek.

Industry observers note that the best use of Pennsylvania rocks I’ve seen so far. You could be one of these every 10 feet.

Pleased with this pitch, not an easy feat in a pile of rocks.

Total: 27.6 miles, 55,557 steps.

I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am latest to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

#91265. Industry News: Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1109 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1109 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like.
  • Sources indicate that it wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change.
  • Recent findings suggest that but it’s not just in my area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like. When I was a kid, more than 1 million hunters would enter the woods and hunt Pennsylvania’s opening day of rifle season. In my heavily populated area, I always saw a lot more hunters than I did deer.

Sources indicate that it wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change. The deer population was skyrocketing and it hasn’t slowed down. Paired with a decline in the hunting population, I’ve experienced the highest deer numbers of my life recently.

Recent findings suggest that but it’s not just in my area. The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags. Tack on the crazy advancements in technology like cellular trail cameras, the latest crossbows, and even technologically-advanced compound bows, and I truly believe deer hunting has never been easier than right now. Here’s why that’s a good thing — sort of.

Across the whitetail’s range, populations are at an all time high. That’s not just my opinion — it’s fact.

Recent findings suggest that “There are between 30 to 35 million whitetails in the U.S. right now,” states Kip Adams, chief conservation officer for the National Deer Association. “That’s a crazy number of deer on the landscape. And, the harvest data is backing that up. Nationally, we’ve only surpassed three million bucks harvested annually four times in the last century, all of which occurred within the last five years. We also have the best age structure in the last 100 years. So we’re killing more bucks, and older bucks than ever before.”.

The good news here is that the increasing population has been met with increases in opportunity from the tag allocation side, and the harvest data proves those opportunities are working.

Industry observers note that “We have expanded seasons across the board, higher bag limits than any point in the last century, and more advanced weapons to fill those tags,” says Adams. “If you can’t shoot a deer today, you just really aren’t trying very hard.”.

Now, before you go grabbing your pitchforks because you’re still sitting on a pile of tags this season, it’s worth mentioning that Adams and I both agreed that it’s never been easier to kill any deer, but we’re certainly not implying it’s easy to kill a specific deer.

According to recent reports, it’s also worth noting that certain areas across the whitetail’s range have seen a decrease in opportunities as diseases like CWD and EHD have impacted herd numbers, and habitat loss continues with urban expansion. But, for most of the whitetail’s range, opportunities abound.

I’ll be the first to admit I love my cell cameras. I check them almost too often this time of year, but that immediate satisfaction and data grab is addicting. And, that data has helped me dial in the movement patterns of the deer herd in my area based on weather conditions in ways that standard SD card cameras couldn’t. That information, when applied correctly, makes filling a tag substantially easier than just guessing and trying to get lucky.

It has been revealed that take the buck my father tagged last year for example. We had gotten a few photos of him in velvet, keying us in on the area he was using. After planning to stay out of the area and wait for mid to late October when the buck started hitting scrapes, we sat back and waited. Around Oct. 21, we got our first photo of him in the area. And he stayed consistent for three days, hitting the scrape every evening in daylight. On the fourth night, we went in, set up, and a shot opportunity presented itself.

Sure, the stars had to align and the conditions had to be just right for that pattern to exist, but without the technological advancements to trail cameras, I don’t know if we would have gotten a chance at that buck.

Sources indicate that tack on the advancements in our gear. From compounds to crossbows, inlines to straight-walls, and even modern cartridge design, we’ve never been better equipped to shoot deer with more accuracy and efficacy.

Recent findings suggest that “Almost all states in the whitetail’s range allow crossbows for everyone now,” Adams notes. “Plus, more and more states that used to be shotgun only are now allowing straight-wall cartridges or inline muzzleloaders. All of those additions make it easier for hunters to fill their tags.”.

While the pros speak for themselves, the cons come down to more of an opinion than anything rooted in fact. I have to wonder what all this ease is doing to the heritage of hunting. Hunting was never about being easy, in fact, I’d argue the opposite. It was about the thrill of the chase, the reward of filling your tag after a long season, putting your woodsmanship to the test and coming out on top, and the conservation of one of America’s most valuable resources.

Sources indicate that I grew to love hunting because it was challenging. I was unsuccessful a lot, which put a fire in my belly to learn more, hunt harder, and find a way to be successful through the lessons I learned along the way. I wonder if kids like me are getting the same experience, and what the hook for them might be if not.

In a recent development, there’s also the ethical dilemma that an easier hunting experience brings. From the ethics and fair-chase argument relating to cellular trail cameras, to the liberal weapon usage and even baiting tactics in certain states, I fear we’re very close to crossing the line into an unfair advantage over our quarry, if we haven’t gotten there already.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

It’s up to us as the hunters, and up to the states to decide how much is too much of a good thing. And as the deer populations continue to expand, I personally don’t see a world where the states are the ones that are going to draw the line. So, this season, as you continue to chase that big buck or a nice doe for the freezer, ask yourself where you plan to draw the line. And, feel free to join me in wondering how it’s still possible to struggle to fill a tag from time to time.

Breaking: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (599 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he remarked.

In a recent development, lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

It has been revealed that neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

The Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch looks to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

This is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Sources indicate that kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

In a recent development, simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his intends while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.
