#91260. The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1234 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1234 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • Industry observers note that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It showed again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

Industry observers note that what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

Sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

After 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang remarked: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Recent findings suggest that several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Recent findings suggest that strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

According to recent reports, “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

“Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

Recent findings suggest that when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

In a recent development, during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s plan to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

Sources indicate that on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

“Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

It has been revealed that “Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

In a recent development, “We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang stated. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

Strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

The climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

The problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Sources indicate that climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Industry observers note that strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

Strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Industry observers note that strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he claims:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

It has been revealed that the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

#91258. ‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (603 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer.
  • “We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life.
  • It was clear this was the season to try to kill him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

“We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”.

It was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

Recent findings suggest that “I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” says Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”.

It has been revealed that the Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

In a recent development, “The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack says. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”.

Industry observers note that zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

Industry observers note that the buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

“When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”.

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he notes.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

“It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack notes. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”.

The deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

Although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

Read Next: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck.

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” indicates Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”.

Finding The Hidden Door on the Camino

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yesterday’s temperature hit nearly 89°F as we left the official Variante Espiritual route and climbed up the mountain to our albergue in the tiny farming hamlet of Silva.
  • There were no restaurants or stores in Silva, but we woke up to find a wonderful breakfast spread mysteriously delivered to the shared kitchen overnight by the owners.
  • The morning was cool, though the sun was warming up fast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yesterday’s temperature hit nearly 89°F as we left the official Variante Espiritual route and climbed up the mountain to our albergue in the tiny farming hamlet of Silva. We were perched about 1.5 km above the Armenteira Monastery, which sat tucked in the valley cove below. Our albergue felt more like a quaint six-room boutique hotel—fully booked, though we somehow never saw another pilgrim.

There were no restaurants or stores in Silva, but we woke up to find a wonderful breakfast spread mysteriously delivered to the shared kitchen overnight by the owners. Fueled up on coffee, tea, pastries, and savory bites, we hit the trail at 9:00 AM.

The morning was cool, though the sun was warming up fast. Although we felt a slight touch of FOMO, we’ve already explored so many spectacular cathedrals and monasteries on this trip that we decided to bypass the descent down into Armenteira, saving ourselves the steep climb back out.

It has been revealed that our morning began with a peaceful walk through the forest up a steep, winding paved road to the hilltop village of Villar. Looking to our right, we could see the stone Monastery of Armenteira nestled deep in the valley cove below.

Looking back and down behind us, the landscape opened up dramatically:.

Knockerz joked that this mountain range was just one giant PUD (Pointless Up and Down). The narrow, winding streets of Villar were flanked by high ancient stone walls shielding medieval houses and barns.

Following our custom Google Maps route, we aimed to rejoin the official Variante Espiritual in the high forest just before the mountain pass.

In a recent development, entering the shaded forest, the path turned into a steep gravel track. Along the way, we stumbled upon four horses grazing freely alongside the road. Farmers here often turn their livestock out to free-range in the high mountain forests.

Soon after passing the horses, we officially rejoined the Variante Espiritual trail as it climbed up from the monastery. We pushed up to the highest point of the pass, where the forest canopy suddenly broke to reveal sweeping views of the Atlantic Ocean far below.

Right off the trail during our descent, we took a break to explore a fascinating historic site featuring ancient stone petroglyphs carved into the bedrock.

Recent findings suggest that continuing down through a recently clear-cut section of forest with wide-open coastal views, a Belgian hiker suddenly popped out of nowhere right in front of us. He had just scrambled straight up the edge of a sheer drop-off. He gave us a sheepish grin and admitted he had taken a “cheat route”—climbing straight up the clear-cut hill instead of following the long, winding switchbacks.

It has been revealed that we took one look at his shortcut and decided we liked the idea. We dropped over the rim and scrambled straight down the mountain along rough logging tracks:.

At the bottom of the slope, we safely reconnected with the official Camino trail.

We stepped out of the woods into an upscale residential neighborhood built directly into the steep hillside. Beautifully kept homes lined narrow alleyways paved with cobblestones. As usual, local Spaniards kept trying to point us in the opposite direction, convinced we were going the wrong way. Once again, we appreciated their deep-rooted tradition of looking out for pilgrims.

Reaching the coastline, we officially said goodbye to the Variante Espiritual and reconnected with the main Portuguese Coastal Camino.

Recent findings suggest that the path shifted to a sidewalk running along a busy coastal road. Although we were hot and out of water, the cool salty ocean breeze refreshed our spirits until we found a small fruit market selling ice-cold water.

In a recent development, the official route drifted back inland toward the hills, but since the area was getting more developed and suburban, we chose to stick to the flat coastal highway to avoid another series of “PUDs” into the hillsides. We crossed a massive bridge over the river and entered the bustling city of Pontevedra.

Pontevedra is a large, vibrant city centered around a massive, beautifully preserved medieval core.

In a recent development, navigating the narrow cobblestone streets, Google Maps brought us right into a lively plaza in the heart of the old town. According to the map, our apartment building was right there—yet we couldn’t see an entrance anywhere.

The app was pointing us directly toward an upscale outdoor bar and restaurant crowded with locals enjoying afternoon drinks. A table of well-dressed patrons looked up in utter perplexity as two sweaty, dirt-covered pilgrims wearing backpacks walked right up to their table.

The Discovery: Directly behind their table—hidden in plain sight—was a massive, 12-foot-tall, 6-foot-wide lime-green ancient wooden door.

I punched in the door code, the heavy latch clicked, and we stepped inside a stunning historic building. We climbed the original wooden staircase to our second-floor apartment. The room was breathtaking: 12-foot ceilings, exposed timber beams, stained-glass accents, and floor-to-ceiling patio doors opening over the plaza. It had the distinct historic charm of a classic Bourbon Street apartment in New Orleans.

After dropping our packs and taking long, hot showers, we put on our clean set of clothes and headed out to explore the medieval center.

We settled into a lively neighborhood tapas bar serving fresh pinchos (small, savory open-faced sandwiches):.

After eating, the city quieted down for afternoon siesta. We returned to our apartment, threw open the balcony doors, and relaxed with a glass of wine, watching the quiet streets below.

Day 44 was a great day on the Camino.

That started an idea of a longer term forest bath on the AT. What a long strange trip its been. Any financial donations I get will be used to send out love to other thru hikers a trail magic.

#91254. A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1975 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1975 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great significant-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • The two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a fresh route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great significant-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

The two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a fresh route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential latest line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

It has been revealed that they climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

It has been revealed that they called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Recent findings suggest that later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

According to recent reports, three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

According to recent reports, was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

In a recent development, one thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

It has been revealed that can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

In a recent development, the two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

Another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

According to recent reports, here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

Recent findings suggest that at the moment, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

How many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

In a recent development, during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

It has been revealed that we had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive big walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

Recent findings suggest that are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

In a recent development, yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

Sources indicate that patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Recent findings suggest that climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

The granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

Sources indicate that there were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

From there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

In a recent development, at the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

It has been revealed that all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

As in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

How much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

Industry observers note that the most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a new route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

It has been revealed that your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

It has been revealed that most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other big-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (574 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road.
  • While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat complications, the recent development is creating even more consternation.
  • “It’s unprecedented,” indicates Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat complications, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

“It’s unprecedented,” indicates Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”.

In a recent development, the proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

The hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves states.

The Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, notes Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner revealed another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves states, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”.

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

The road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has mentioned he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

Read Next: The Ambler Road Project Would Jeopardize One of the Last Great Wilderness Hunts in America.

According to recent reports, “There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”.

#91248. Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (791 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Sources indicate that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

The skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

It has been revealed that the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

It has been revealed that other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police remarked the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

Avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident shows that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

The accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

The avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

The second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the big powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them plan to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

It has been revealed that snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) indicates low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

In a recent development, the avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps highlights remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.

#91244. Latest Update: Arizona Trail: Part 4

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Arizona Trail: Part 4

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2431 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the transition from a double zero back to the trail was especially tough this time around because I was sick.
  • I stuffed my red bandana, now officially my snot rag, into the water bottle holder on the side of my backpack and set off.
  • According to recent reports, with my trusty snot rag in hand, I slowly climbed the mountain, with stunning views gradually revealing themselves along the way.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the transition from a double zero back to the trail was especially tough this time around because I was sick. Seppo and Emma had both come down with colds, and after sleeping next to them in a garage at a trail angel’s house, it seemed the sickness had made its way to me too. It was funny because up until that point, I had been finding the trail relatively easy. The terrain was mostly cruisy, and we weren’t hiking huge miles. I tried to convince myself that getting a cold was just a fun little extra challenge to add to the trail.

I stuffed my red bandana, now officially my snot rag, into the water bottle holder on the side of my backpack and set off. Everyone had already left camp, but I was moving a little slower given the circumstances. I quickly caught up to Alex on an uphill, who had somehow remained unaware that we were gaining 5,000 feet that morning. After breaking the news to him, I continued on.

According to recent reports, with my trusty snot rag in hand, I slowly climbed the mountain, with stunning views gradually revealing themselves along the way. As I crested the ridgeline, I noticed some concerning dark clouds hovering nearby. Before long, I found myself caught in a mixture of hail and rain. I spotted Seppo and Emma up ahead, who had found a lovely log to sit on. By the time I joined them and started eating lunch, the rain had stopped, giving me a chance to pull out my tent and let it dry.

It has been revealed that alex showed up a little while later, and we were both feeling pretty tired and less than thrilled about the morning’s events. After a long lunch break, we continued on, heading back down all the elevation we had just worked so hard to gain. Some people might refer to this as “pointless ups and downs,” or PUDs for short, but I like to think of it as the trail making us work for Mexico.

Sources indicate that we moseyed along all afternoon, moving at barely 2 mph despite the fact that it was all downhill. Alex and I chatted about an assortment of topics, ranging from our dream of opening a guiding business to his attempts to teach me about the stock market. As the sun began to set, we decided to aim for the next good campsite. The only problem was that the next good campsite never seemed to come. The terrain was incredibly slanted, and after passing a spot that was barely half the size of our tent and deciding we didn’t want to attempt squeezing into it, we pulled out our headlamps and kept going.

Recent findings suggest that we eventually made it to 21.4 miles before calling it a day at one of the most crowded campsites we’d seen on trail so far. Clearly, we weren’t the only ones struggling to find a decent place to sleep. We squeezed our tent in among eight others, trying to be as quiet as possible since it was already 7 p.m., dark, and everyone else seemed to be fast asleep.

Recent findings suggest that when I woke up the next morning, I was unsurprisingly still tired and sick. But the sun was shining, and we had 12 downhill miles to cover before lunch. I plugged in my earbuds, put on some Noah Kahan, and started hiking. The halfway mark was calling.

Industry observers note that up ahead, I spotted Kayla, Seppo, and Emma already working on building the 400-mile marker out of rocks. After taking some pictures and celebrating the halfway point, we continued on, the sun warming us with every step.

The day before, Alex had told me that this was the hardest part of the hike for him. We had just as much trail ahead of us as we had already completed, and that felt daunting. He felt like he was ONLY halfway. I, on the other hand, was feeling sad because we WERE halfway. Having already completed two trails of over 2,000 miles each, this trail was feeling a little too short for my liking. I never wanted it to end.

It has been revealed that later that afternoon, we passed a group of cows that mooed loudly at us before we began another climb. As I gained elevation, the sun started to set, and Emma and I took turns setting the pace up the switchbacks. Seppo and Kayla had booked it up the climb, eager to reach camp before sunset, while we could see Alex far below, just beginning the switchbacks as we approached the ridgeline.

The sunset was gorgeous. With the days getting shorter, we now had the privilege of watching both the sunrise and sunset every single day. This one was especially spectacular. Emma and I kept stopping to take pictures as the sky shifted from orange to pink to purple. With half a mile left to camp, Emma went ahead while I waited for Alex. We finally arrived just as the sun dipped below the horizon.

Industry observers note that our campsite was perched on the side of a hill, and the colorful sky soon gave way to a blanket of sparkling stars. We sat in a circle on the ground, eating dinner and enjoying the evening. It was my favorite campsite of the trail so far.

The next morning, we watched the sunrise over Lake Roosevelt as we made our way down a dirt road. The first 11 miles of the day were spent walking along dirt roads, which are actually some of my favorite miles on trail. I find dirt roads so fun and exciting, which is quite a hot take among thru-hikers. There’s just something about the monotony of a dirt road, kicking up dust with every step and occasionally having an ATV drive by, that makes me feel like a cowboy. Dirt road miles also tend to fly by much quicker than trail miles, and the morning seemed to disappear in no time.

It has been revealed that we stopped for a quick lunch at a creek before continuing on. Unfortunately, the afternoon was quite the opposite of the morning and brought some of my least favorite terrain on the trail. It was beautiful, but we spent much of the afternoon walking along washed-out cliffs, with the trail precariously carved into the mountainside. Progress was slow, but I put on some podcasts and tried to zone out rather than overthink just how slowly I was moving.

Eventually, I made it to camp and set up our tent on a lovely patch of sandy ground. Once the sun went down, the temperature dropped swiftly, and I was more than grateful to crawl into my sleeping bag for the night.

In a recent development, in the morning, we crossed into the Four Peaks Wilderness and began descending into the low desert. The terrain slowly shifted from high desert shrubs to towering saguaro cacti stretching as far as I could see. Our first saguaros of the trail! This was exactly what I had imagined the entire Arizona Trail would look like. Of course, within the first two days of hiking, I had already realized that wasn’t quite the case. Maybe I should do a little more research before setting off on these trails. Still, I was so stoked to finally be surrounded by some of the oldest cacti in the world.

Industry observers note that as we neared the road crossing and our next resupply point, I spotted a black truck with a white camper parked nearby. It looked strangely familiar, and when I reached the road, I realized it was Kayla’s husband doing trail magic! He whipped up smoothies for us, and we happily feasted on fruit and soda. I can confidently say that smoothie was some of the best trail magic I’ve ever had.

After saying our thanks, we headed over to the Lake Roosevelt Marina for a rather unconventional resupply. The marina was stocked with food geared more toward boaters than thru-hikers, but I managed to make it work. We grabbed a quick burger at the restaurant before heading back out onto the trail. Three miles later, we found a spot to call home for the night.

Immediately after leaving camp that morning, we entered a wash and followed it for the first couple miles of the day. The trail through this section was heavily overgrown with spiky bushes, so we decided to follow the more open wash instead. It turned out to be quite fun, weaving our way through the canyon with cacti growing all around us. It felt like a little adventure of its own. The path had been carved out by flowing water over countless years, and we got to walk along the dry remains of that process, making our way over sand and gravel through the canyon.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, the wash narrowed, and we hopped onto a dirt road that led us back to the trail. The road was steep, and we trudged uphill under the exposed sun. After what felt like ages, I finally crested the ridgeline and found myself walking along relatively flat ground, with views stretching out in every direction. It was stunning, but I was having a hard time appreciating the beauty. I was tired and just wasn’t feeling it. I stopped to dump the rocks out of my shoes, and Alex caught up with me. We decided to take a lunch break in the shade. After shoving a tortilla stuffed with pepperoni, cheese, and crushed sour cream and onion chips into my dry mouth, we continued on.

Industry observers note that the afternoon was just as hard as the morning. We continued climbing deeper into the Superstition Mountains, at one point gaining 1,000 feet in just over a mile. It was absolutely brutal, and both Alex and I ran out of water. It was the only time that happened during the entire trail. Eventually, we reached some cruisy downhill, but by then, it was too late. The sun was setting, we’d managed just fifteen miles in nine hours, and I was completely exhausted. We decided to call it an early day and scrolled through the FarOut comments, looking for a flat spot to camp a little farther ahead.

It has been revealed that by the time Alex and I arrived at the campsite in the dark, all of our friends and fellow thru-hikers were already set up. It turned out we weren’t the only ones who had struggled that day. Everyone agreed that the 17 miles that day had been the hardest on trail so far.

In a recent development, I woke up grumpy, with the difficulties of the previous day still weighing on my mood. Luckily, the miles came much easier that morning, and I quickly walked myself out of my funk. There was another storm on the way, the weekly plague of Super El Niño looming over us. Before dropping down into the low desert, I checked the weather report using the lingering one bar of cell service I had. Rain, rain, and more rain. There were over four inches of rain predicted over the following three days. Not exactly ideal hiking weather.

It has been revealed that my brain immediately went into problem-solving mode. What dirt roads could we bail out on? Could we flip south, where the weather might be less severe? Could we road walk along the highway? I didn’t want to take a triple zero, but I also didn’t want to put myself in a dangerous situation by attempting to hike through flash flooding and thunderstorms.

In a recent development, I came up with a initiative and proposed it to Alex, Seppo, and Emma. What if we hiked into town that day, did a super quick resupply and laundry, then hiked out early the following morning? We could crush some miles over the next two days and hopefully reach the next town before the worst of the storm hit. To my surprise, everyone agreed to my slightly crazy plan. I think we were all getting pretty tired of taking zero days just to wait out the storms.

According to recent reports, we reached a dirt road crossing, where we met Ace and his dog Charlie. Ace made us pizza and gave us beer before we headed off to walk the last couple of miles into Superior. Little did I know that Ace would become such an crucial part of my Arizona Trail experience, but that’s a story for a later blog….

Recent findings suggest that we had the most efficient town stop of my thru-hiking career. It certainly helped that Superior is a tiny town, with pretty much everything a hiker could need within a quarter-mile walk of the motel. We arrived at the motel around 7 p.m. and immediately got to work. We threw our laundry in the washing machine, walked to a Mexican restaurant for dinner, then headed back to the motel to switch everything into the dryer. Next, we walked to Family Dollar to resupply for the next two days. Back at the motel, we collected our clean laundry, showered, and were fast asleep by 10 p.m. Pretty efficient, right?

In a recent development, I fell asleep scrolling through weather reports and studying topo maps of the next section, trying to find potential campsites that weren’t too high and exposed in case of thunderstorms, but also weren’t too low in case of flash flooding. I was nervous, but also excited. Another adventure was just around the corner.

It has been revealed that today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police unveiled that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

His two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

Recent findings suggest that ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

#91242. The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3824 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3824 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “I Shot Big Red,” appeared in the January 1967 concern of Outdoor Life.
  • At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime.
  • It has been revealed that I might as well quit, I thought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “I Shot Big Red,” appeared in the January 1967 concern of Outdoor Life. Shelton’s buck is now the 20th biggest typical whitetail ever taken in Kentucky, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. At the time, however, it was the biggest ever taken in Kentucky. It also had a wider inside and outside spread than any deer on the books, including the then-world-record deer.

At 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime. The rain, which had been steady since before dawn, suddenly stopped, and the woods of northern Todd County, Kentucky, were still. I was 20 feet up in a huge sycamore, watching a deer runway that meandered through thick brush. I’d been half-wet most of the day, and I felt another case of chills coming on.

It has been revealed that I might as well quit, I thought. I’m not going to see Big Red, and I probably won’t see any other deer.

In a recent development, my thoughts seemed logical, but another line of reasoning wouldn’t be denied. This was Todd County’s first deer season in modern times, and the season was for this day only. So far as Significant Red was concerned, I had good reason to believe he was the best trophy whitetail buck in North America. Besides, I’m mighty stubborn when it comes to deer hunting. I decided to stay in that tree till dark.

Industry observers note that in front of me, to the north and 30 yards away, a tiny creek flowed through a heavily wooded east-west valley. The runway crossed the creek and continued into dense thickets. I couldn’t see the thickets’ far edge, but I knew the growth thinned against a hillside that topped out alongside a stubble cornfield 200 yards away. The cornfield was 40 yards wide and bordered a little-used gravel road. Across the road was 40 acres of tangled cedars, the thickest cover in the area. I figured any deer leaving those cedars would use the runway I was watching.

In a recent development, around 2:30 a twig snapped behind me, to the south. Then I heard branches rubbing together and sounds resembling a squirrel digging in the ground. I knew I was listening to a deer.

The sounds were a few yards off the runway. In another minute they became more distinguishable, and I knew the animal was working toward me. I had two choices: remain motionless in hopes the deer would move past me, or try to inch my way around so I’d face south.

Though the leaves were off the trees, I figured I had an excellent chance of moving without being seen. I was standing on a huge branch, but I was tight against the trunk. Deer don’t normally look up, so I also had that advantage. In addition, I figured the deer was feeding and not alerted to immediate danger. I moved as cautiously as possible.

It took a few minutes to make my move. Now I was facing south. Surprisingly, I could still hear the same sounds, but I couldn’t see any movement.

The sounds kept coming closer. Then, as if by magic, there he was. I saw antlers and legs at the same instant, about 30 yards away. The buck was pawing at acorns. I couldn’t get a clear view of his antlers, and I didn’t dare risk a shot through that thick brush. There wasn’t much I could do except wait.

After what seemed like hours, he suddenly tossed his head up. He seemed to be looking straight at me. His rack was massive, but I knew instantly it didn’t belong to Big Red. I was sure the buck had caught a glimpse of me or winded me.

I better take him, I thought. Time is running out.

My .44 Magnum Ruger carbine was braced against the trunk. I started lining the crosswires of my Weaver scope on his chest. Then, through my variable-power scope, I made an amazing discovery. That buck wasn’t looking up at me at all; he was staring on the level along the runway toward the north.

Industry observers note that now the eight-pointer relaxed and dropped his head to feed again. I heard the same sounds that had startled him. To the north, behind me now, I heard another deer. I glanced over my shoulder and got the second biggest shock of my life. Big Red, in all his glory, was walking toward my tree stand. The monstrous buck was in clear view, 50 yards away and moving down the runway. There was no question about his identity.

Recent findings suggest that I had seen him two years ago when we had come face to face under the most dramatic conditions. We had startled each other that time. Now I had all the cards. Or did I? I was in no position to shoot. If that buck was alerted to the slightest suspicion, he’d bound into the thickets and disappear.

It has been revealed that this dream situation had been in the making for a long time. I guess it really started when I was nine years old, the day I shot my first squirrel. After stalking the gray for hours, I knocked it off a stump with my brother Rudy’s .22. I decided then and there I wanted to become the world’s best hunter. That boyhood ambition has never dimmed, though it’s been realistically tempered by maturity. At that time my family lived in the town of Mayfield, in southwestern Kentucky. There was plenty of small game and birds, but no deer.

By the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

By the time I was in high school, I was addicted to duck hunting. The area around Mayfield is laced with creeks, rivers, and potholes. It was a duck paradise. I taught myself how to call by sneaking up on flocks of waterfowl and listening to their various calls. I’d go hunting before and after school every day during the season. I practically lived outdoors. But by the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

Industry observers note that I’m 26 now and live in Bowling Green, where I work as a real estate salesman and auctioneer. My wife and I have a daughter, four, and a son, two.

Kentucky’s first modern deer season opened in 1956, when I was still a teenager. I didn’t get a chance to hunt deer until 1959, but nobody ever dreamed about deer hunting more than I did.

Looking back, I realize I started my first season as quite a stupid deer hunter. I had no experience, and I’d never seen a deer in my life. The 1959 season lasted three days, and I hunted every one of them from dawn to dark. After it was all over, my record was unblemished: I still hadn’t seen a deer. I’m not sure I even saw a fresh track.

It has been revealed that three months before the 1960 season opened, I started scouting my hunting territory on weekends. With six weeks to go, I stepped up my scouting trips to every couple of days. I found runways and beds, examined browse conditions, and located the “use” areas of three herds of whitetails. It all paid off. I killed a fat doe from a tree stand just after dawn on the opening day of the season.

It has been revealed that I missed the 1961 season because of a session with Uncle Sam, but I didn’t lose contact with shooting. My ability with a rifle was good enough to win me an instructor’s rating, and I had charge of an army rifle range for 10 months.

Recent findings suggest that in 1962 and 1963, I collected my second and third whitetails. I shot both of them while sneaking silently into bedding areas I’d discovered on scouting trips. My 1962 deer bolted from thick brush 80 yards away, and I dropped him with a single bullet. My third deer, a six-pointer, heard me pussyfooting along, but I saw him before he spotted me. He went down in his tracks.

According to recent reports, after I killed my first deer, I studied taxidermy and began mounting deer heads for my friends. I mounted the head of my substantial six-pointer, but every time I looked at it I dreamed of the day when those six points would be dwarfed by a much larger rack. My dream had plenty of substance because by this time I’d seen Big Red.

We met in October, 1962, while I was living in the town of Elkton, Todd County. I’d heard that the county might be opened to deer hunting, so I started scouting likely areas. I’d done some business with H. Sweeney, a local farmer, and he’d told me he frequently saw deer crossing his fields.

Industry observers note that on one of my scouting trips, I found a heavily traveled runway through a hilly area of oak, poplar, hickory, and cedar. The runway was pocked with fresh tracks, and I followed it down through the hills and across a valley to where it led into a rye field. Where the field met the woods, a huge oak tree offered a perfect stand. I decided to climb the tree and see what moved along the runway toward evening.

It has been revealed that about 5 p.m. I heard some deer coming through the woods. It was a warm, quiet day, and the trees were still in full foliage, so I heard them for a long time before I saw them. Shortly, three deer walked below me and went out into the rye field to feed. I watched them for half an hour. Then I heard another deer. He moved steadily to the last bit of cover, then stopped.

Industry observers note that I made out the partial outline of a huge deer. The whitetail stood motionless for a full five minutes; then he stepped into the field and joined the other animals. He had an eight-point rack and was the biggest deer I’d ever seen.

Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Then I heard dogs barking. They were chasing something, and the sounds kept coming closer. A six-point buck suddenly burst out of the woods, ran under my tree, and joined the other deer. As if on signal, they all bolted out of sight.

I never did see the dogs or any more deer, though I stayed in the tree till dusk. I’d traveled farther than I thought, and it was dark before I got halfway back to my car. I decided to bypass the woods and stay in the fields. It was this decision that set up the chance meeting with Big Red.

Industry observers note that I was crossing a fescue field when I approached a man-made stock pond. Banks, about 10 feet high, had been bulldozed around the pond to collect and hold water. I could have walked around the embankment, but I decided to walk along the top of it. A full moon had just cleared the horizon, and the landscape was bathed with an eerie beauty. I went up to the top of the bank and got the shock of my life. Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

The huge animal was silhouetted against the moon in fantastic beauty. I guess we saw each other in the same instant, and we both froze, each sizing up the other.

According to recent reports, I remember my breath going out in a gasp. My first thought was that I was looking at somebody’s tame elk. Then I knew the animal had to be a deer. His size didn’t awe me so much as did the tremendous spread of his antlers.

We must have stared at each other for seconds. Then the monster buck snorted, whirled, and bolted down the bank and across the field. About 75 yards away, he leaped a five-foot fence. Then he stopped and looked back. I took a few steps toward him, and he trotted into some woods.

I was talking to myself when I got back to the farmer’s yard where I’d parked my car. I went up to the house and knocked on the door. He didn’t seem very impressed when I exclaimed, “I’ve just seen the biggest buck in Kentucky!”.

“That’s Significant Red,” he said. “I’ve seen him a few times. You can’t mistake him. He’s a lot bigger than an ordinary deer. His face is sort of reddish. That’s why we call him Big Red. The local farmers know about him, and you’re going to have plenty of company if you figure on hunting that buck.”.

In a recent development, as it turned out, Todd County wasn’t open for deer hunting in 1962 or 1963. Kentucky controls its whitetail population by allowing hunting only in counties where the herds have built up to the carrying capacity of available deer range. In 1956 (the first year that deer hunting had been allowed since 1911) only 27 of the state’s 120 counties were open to shooting. In that season 6,000 hunters killed 1,300 whitetails. By comparison, 14,000 hunters bagged 4,100 deer in 1965. The 1966 population was estimated at well over 50,000 deer, and hunting was allowed in 74 counties.

All of this had its beginning in 1950 when the state began its stocking program with deer bought from Pennsylvania. Original stockings were made in Mammoth Cave National Park and Federal Wildlife refuges. With a ban on hunting, these herds multiplied so rapidly that certain areas became overrun with deer. Live-trapping crews thinned out the overpopulated sections and stocked the deer in other areas that had heavy browse conditions. As these herds build to huntable populations, additional counties are opened to hunting.

In the summer of 1964, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources declared that Todd County would have its first deer season, a one-day hunt on November 28. I told my brother Rudy about Big Red, and we planned to hunt him together. We didn’t get much sleep the night before the season opened, and we left for our hunting area at 3 a.m.

A few changes had taken place during the two years since I’d met Substantial Red. The monster buck had moved from the Sweeney farm to adjoining woodlands owned by farmer Ross Laster. The deer’s travel routes had also changed, but I knew all about this because I knew Ross well and hadn’t relaxed my scouting trips. I hadn’t seen the buck a second time, but I’d found his tracks many times, and some of the local farmers had seen him just a month earlier.

Dawn was breaking when Rudy and I drove down a gravel road toward Ross’s farm. A mile from our destination, a four-point buck jumped across the road ahead of us, ran to the far edge of a small stubble cornfield and stopped.

“Get your rifle and nail him,” Rudy noted as he braked the car.

In a recent development, “No, you take him,” I answered. Neither of us made a move, and the buck walked slowly out of sight. While we wouldn’t admit it, both Rudy and I weren’t the least bit interested in shooting that buck.

We drove to the farmhouse, and Ross had news.

Industry observers note that “That bunch of deer are traveling new runways,” he mentioned. “The best one is about a mile down the road by a cornfield where. . . .”.

“That’s where we just saw a buck,” I interrupted. “There’s a bunch of cedars across the road.”.

Sources indicate that “That’s the place,” Ross said. “I’d forget your other prepares and pick a couple of stands along that runway.”.

It has been revealed that that’s exactly what we did. Half an hour later, I found the substantial sycamore I mentioned in the beginning. Rudy decided to follow the runway toward some heavily wooded ridges half a mile away.

It has been revealed that the air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

Industry observers note that about 8 o’clock, it started raining hard. By 8:30 I was so wet I went back to the car, changed clothes, and put on a yellow rainsuit. I was almost back to the sycamore when I heard shots from Rudy’s area. I walked up on a ridge and found Rudy all excited.

“I shot at a buck with a brushpile rack,” he said. “I was curled up under a tree trying to stay dry when I heard a deer coming down the runway behind me. I turned around and we spotted each other at the same time. The buck bolted, and I cut loose with three shots. I lost his tracks right here. He sure was a big one!”.

Recent findings suggest that rudy was a mighty disappointed deer hunter. He’s 35 and one of the best outdoorsmen I know. He’s been a hunting nut all his life, and he taught me how to hunt and fish when I was a boy. He lives in Mayfield where he works as a heavy-equipment operator. He’s married and has two teenage sons.

In a recent development, rudy went back to his stand, and I stillhunted till noon. We met at the car for lunch, stillhunted another hour, then returned to our stands. It wasn’t long after that when I glanced over my shoulder and saw Big Red.

I don’t remember any trace of buck fever, but I do recall coldly analyzing the situation. I studied every bit of cover between myself and the deer. About 40 yards from my tree stand, a clump of cedars edged the runway. Big Red would have to pass behind that clump. When he did, I’d turn around.

My change in position came off like clockwork. When the animal appeared again he was unsuspicious, and I was in perfect shooting position with my scope lined up on his chest. I decided against squeezing the trigger. I wanted him to come as close as possible.

Industry observers note that at the creek 30 yards away, the trophy buck stopped for a drink. The suspense was terrible. I used this moment of his relaxed alertness to suck in a deep breath. The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

Suddenly he stopped, turned his head toward his backtrack, tilted his nose, and tested the air. Then he swung his massive antlers forward and walked behind a couple of cedars where he stopped dead still. I had a feeling he was getting nervous.

He might bolt at any second, I thought. As soon as he steps from behind those cedars, I’m going to shoot.

Recent findings suggest that the range was now 25 yards, and there was no question about his increased caution. His face peeked from behind the cedars. Then that unbelievable rack. Again he stood motionless. Suddenly he broke into a fast trot.

The crosswires settled at the base of his neck, and my rifle roared.

Sources indicate that substantial Red staggered sideways, regained control of his feet, and lunged straight ahead. I aimed my second shot for his shoulder, and the 240-grain bullet spun him around. He dived into thickets alongside the runway and was gone. I heard him crash through brush; then all was silent. I knew he had fallen.

I went down that tree as fast as I could. I got within 30 yards of him, and then he staggered away. I snapped two shots through the thickets, but the bullets never got to him. I heard him fall again about 60 yards to my right. I got within 40 feet of him before he tried getting up. He couldn’t make it. Another bullet finished him instantly.

Recent findings suggest that I started field-dressing the buck immediately. It wasn’t easy. His bulk was so great I couldn’t move him. I tied his legs to saplings to spread-eagle his hindquarters. Throughout the job, I whistled for Rudy every few minutes. It’s a whistle note we’ve used for woods communication since we were kids. I was nearly done with the chore when Rudy found me. He stayed with the buck while I went to Ross Laster’s farm for help.

Four of the Laster brothers and I got a tractor to within 300 yards of Massive Red. Then we had to chop down saplings, clear brush, and cut a fence to get the tractor within 100 yards of the buck. After that it was pure bull work — dragging, hauling, and lifting Big Red till we finally had him balanced on the tractor.

Sources indicate that A few hours later, he weighed 260 pounds on a coal scale. I was surprised because I’d figured he would scale over 300 pounds. I guess the massive antlers fooled me. I was familiar with the Boone and Crockett Club method of scoring trophy deer, and I was certain my buck would score near the top of the record list.

It has been revealed that two months later, the antlers scored 185 4/8 points. My trophy won third place for typical whitetails in the Boone and Crockett Club two-year competition period ending December 31, 1965. Though I didn’t kill a fresh world record, I did score some impressive ratings. Big Red is the best trophy whitetail ever killed in Kentucky.

In a recent development, the inside spread of his rack measures 30 2/8 inches, more than 10 inches wider than the current world record. While checking the last listing of all-time Boone and Crockett records, I discovered that this inside measurement is the greatest among all typical whitetail deer recorded there. Though I realize that total score is all that counts, I doubt whether anyone will ever kill a whitetail buck with a wider antler spread than Big Red’s.

There’s one thing I can guarantee — nobody will ever know a greater hunting thrill than I experienced when I looked over my shoulder in that sycamore and saw the dream of a lifetime coming true.
