📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the upcoming route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

Recent findings suggest that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

In a recent development, siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

The three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

It has been revealed that sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

Along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

On Shiva, Siegrist claims the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

The climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

It has been revealed that that night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast confirmed a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

The last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

Recent findings suggest that the sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

Tech Report: Lessons I Learned from Deer Hunting with My Kids

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For a span of maybe a dozen years, from when my twin boys were 11 until their kid sister went to college, we together killed an average of six deer a year, mainly bucks but a few antlerless whitetails and mule deer when we needed the meat.
  • According to recent reports, that’s a lot of early mornings in northeastern Montana, a lot of cold feet and wintry weather, and a lot of cutting and wrapping and sausage grinding.
  • What’s most remarkable about my kids’ deer hunting journey is that almost all of it took place on our family’s farm and ranch, which we bought when my boys were 9 years old and which in most years holds a satisfying mix of mule deer in the sagebrush-and-gumbo uplands and whitetails in the irrigated bottomlands.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a span of maybe a dozen years, from when my twin boys were 11 until their kid sister went to college, we together killed an average of six deer a year, mainly bucks but a few antlerless whitetails and mule deer when we needed the meat.

According to recent reports, that’s a lot of early mornings in northeastern Montana, a lot of cold feet and wintry weather, and a lot of cutting and wrapping and sausage grinding. The body count is a poor measure of our experiences together, though, as it doesn’t tally countless blown stalks, missed shots, and those curiously memorable days when we didn’t see anything worth shooting but we found arrowheads and bison skulls and watched waves of sandhill cranes migrate south. Or those days we talked about fickle friends, where grandparents go when they die, and the notion of self-reliance.

What’s most remarkable about my kids’ deer hunting journey is that almost all of it took place on our family’s farm and ranch, which we bought when my boys were 9 years old and which in most years holds a satisfying mix of mule deer in the sagebrush-and-gumbo uplands and whitetails in the irrigated bottomlands.

My kids are freshly gone from the home place. My boys have grown-up jobs in cities on opposite coasts. My daughter is in her first year of graduate school in California.

In the years they’ve been away, I’ve realized how little I care about all the deer-season conversations that used to pique my interest: best days of the rut, the perfect deer caliber, various hacks to unlock locked-up bucks. Instead, I now nourish myself during deer season with a handful of rich lessons accumulated with my kids. If you can excuse the musings of an empty-nest father, here are some of our experiences that still speak to me, years later.

Sources indicate that for a confirmed skeptic, I’ll allow the presence of mystery in many parts of my life. How else can I explain the fact that my wife of 29 years still finds me funny or that the nib of a lead pencil that Eric Thompson stabbed me with back in third grade is still in the roll-over flab of my waistline?

Here’s more evidence of mystery. On my son Ellis’s very first deer hunt, after we decided a mule deer doe would be a great way to begin a long hunting career, we were set up on a cottonwood limb that offered a solid rest for Ellis’s .243. Our little stand overlooked a corner of an alfalfa field that spilled into sagebrush and then into a prairie stream that’s a favorite bedding area for mule deer.

On cue, the deer started filing toward the alfalfa field. Ellis had practiced dry-firing and panning his gun on the branch. Now he was loaded and ready, and, as if scripted, a yearling mule deer walked into view, not 80 yards away, just on the other side of an old barbed-wire fence. Strangely calm as the deer turned broadside to contemplate mule-deery things, Ellis sent one.

Watching from over his shoulder, I expected the deer to crumple, or maybe take the hit and lurch. But the deer just stood there looking at us, and I saw no dust or other evidence of the shot. Now El was rattled.

“What do I do?” he hissed over his shoulder. “Rack another one,” I whispered back. But the deer had had enough and was gone.

According to recent reports, I was sure El had pulled the shot. After all, hadn’t I missed the first couple deer I had shot at when I was his age? It’s natural to be twitchy when confronted for the first time with the reality of taking an animal’s life. Only Ellis insisted that he had been calm and steady.

Industry observers note that “Let’s go make sure you didn’t cut hair or draw any blood,” I noted. Ellis cleared his chamber and we walked toward the first fence, crossed it, and inspected the spot where the deer had been standing when El shot. No blood. No hair. No evidence of a hit. We walked back to our hide, and that’s when I saw it, a freshly clipped vertical cross wire in the first fence.

Industry observers note that ellis went back to the cottonwood limb, and used a straight stick to line up where his rifle had pointed at the deer. It was perfectly aligned with the fence. His .243-caliber bullet had cut the .150-inch-diameter wire, deflecting his shot and saving that deer.

On the way back to the house, Ellis seemed to metabolize the events that had just unfolded.

“Maybe there’s a reason I missed,” he mused. “Maybe it wasn’t time. Maybe I’ll find that deer later.”.

Industry observers note that I have no way of knowing if any of the future mule deer Ellis killed descended from that lucky yearling, but in the years since, I’ve hit limbs instead of vitals, had bullets deflect off unseen sagebrush, and once had an eagle spook a dandy buck just as I was about to shoot. It’s the hidden hand of happenstance. Some people call it fate. Some call it luck. Whenever it happens to me, it conjures Ellis and the pigtailed wire that spoiled his first sure-thing hunt.

Recent findings suggest that ellis’s twin brother, Merlin, is the most coachable kid I’ve known, and I say that as a longtime coach of track and cross-country runners, some of whom are not related to me. Merlin listens well, follows directions, and is committed to a shared outcome.

So it baffled me just a little when, after graduating from Montana’s Hunter Education course and living under my tutelage about the proper place to shoot a deer, he proceeded to take a neck shot on his first deer.

The doe went about 3 feet, straight down. Lucky, I told him. A few inches high or low and you miss. A couple inches right, you blow the jaw off and the deer dies a horrible death, ultimately of starvation. But Merlin correctly noted that a proper neck shot saves a lot of meat.

His next couple deer also fell to neck shots. Every time, I reminded him of the risks of the shot, and about the forgiveness of the “boiler room” behind the front shoulder that takes out both lungs and maybe the top of the heart.

In a recent development, merlin’s rifle was a Ruger No. 1 single-shot chambered in .243. It’s not the most accurate rifle in my collection, but Merlin shot it well, and over the years I came to learn that he had supreme confidence in that gun, and in his one-and-done shot. It’s not my nature to stay quiet — especially when I’m right — but I piped down, and was quietly overjoyed to skin and butcher deer that had four intact quarters and no internal injuries.

Industry observers note that I came to realize that Merlin knew something I didn’t. He knew precisely where he was sending that bullet, because he wouldn’t take a shot outside the proficiency zone of his gun and his abilities. When a shot exceeded that distance, he aimed for the boiler room. I came to recognize that his quiet belief in his own abilities has given Merlin opportunities that might never come to a blustery self-promoter.

Recent findings suggest that it was hard to know if hunting would take hold of Iris after her first year. She was a little tentative, in part because we hired a videographer to document her experiences – you can watch it here. Who subjects an 11-year-old girl to that indignity? But despite her initial reluctance, Iris became the most dedicated and determined hunter of my three kids. And, especially after my boys went on to college, hunting was something we shared and nurtured.

According to recent reports, but Iris was burdened by an unseen weight that I’ve observed in other hunters, especially in women and girls. She was so cautious about making a perfect shot that she sometimes allowed otherwise pretty good opportunities to dissolve and then evaporate as she waited for the platonic textbook broadside.

I’ve learned from a lifetime in the field and elsewhere that perfection sometimes isn’t clear in the moment. It can be vanishingly quick to come and go, so quick that many of us scarcely notice it. That quartering-away shot that exposes the vitals of a buck is nearly as good as a broadside shot, I might argue, but Iris was deaf to my suggestions that she relax her standards in this single situation.

Happily, as she’s grown older, Iris has relaxed her expectations while maintaining her high standards. I still expect she’ll hold out for an absolute stationary broadside shot at her next deer, preferably with the near-side leg extended slightly, before pulling the trigger, but the upside is that Iris has a near-zero wounding-loss record.

As an imperfect human, who am I to encourage less of anyone, especially my one and only daughter? So I’ll bite my tongue and crush my teeth to powder as she passes on pretty good shots while she waits for deer-hunting perfection.

Sources indicate that I recognize too late that I was a tyrannical hunting mentor to my kids. If they failed to do things my way, I became a hard-hearted scold. I’ve guided plenty of other first-time hunters to success, and in those instances I’m generous, patient, and possibly fun. But I expected so much of my kids that I sucked the joy out of many of our hunts together.

Industry observers note that ellis was the first to go. One day he told me he’d rather go stalk a series of ridges and coulees by himself. That first experience in going it alone became the norm. Later that season, I headed out with the other kids to hunt elk in the Missouri Breaks, but Ellis remarked he’d stay back on the ranch and try to scratch out a deer.

Industry observers note that we returned after dark to find the house dark and no sign of Ellis. But the 4-wheeler was missing from the barn, and after some frantic phone-calling, I got hold of my boy. He had shot a deer, he mentioned, way across the ranch, and his friend Brett had come to help, but now they were lost in the dark. I got a fix on their location and drove my own 4-wheeler to the spot. The headlights illuminated a crime scene. Blood covered nearly an acre of sagebrush, and then Ellis came into view. Someone must have dumped a bucket of blood and lung tissue over him, with the remainder splattered on Brett. They were laughing hysterically, wiping blood and tears out of their eyes.

It has been revealed that it was the worst field dressing I’ve ever seen, but nobody cared. Ellis had done it. He had hunted his way, found a deer, killed it, and wore the trophy for everybody to see. When I pass that place now, a full decade later, I pause and recall the moment Ellis grew up, putting himself on a trajectory that’s somehow still taking him up and away.

Iris was in her first years of hunting when Chronic Wasting Disease was first detected in our county. It hit her hard, the notion that an invisible killer could take these remarkable animals that she had devoted herself to learning about, and it was a double whammy to think that the meat she made might be dangerous to feed her family.

Sources indicate that so in the first years of CWD monitoring, Iris insisted that we test every deer we shot. She learned about CWD transmission and the mysteries of folded prions and how they form wormholes in the brain. She learned how to extract lymph nodes from our deer. When we hunted, she watched deer for signs of sickness. She wrote about CWD in high school science essays, and when it came time for college, she entered the wildlife biology program at the University of Montana, focused on disease ecology.

Read Next, by the Same Author: An Old-School Western Mule Deer Hunt in Memory of Two Midwestern Dads.

It has been revealed that now in graduate school, she’s expanded her gaze to include other wildlife diseases that have the potential to infect humans. She’s learning how to develop vaccines and studying the importance of healthy ecosystems as the first defense against disease.

And she can’t wait to return next week to hunt with me, to rekindle the spark of discovery that began when she was a little girl behind binoculars, watching deer and deciding if they looked delicious enough to take home.

Two Inexperienced Teens Rescued After 20 Hours on Grossglockner

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
  • Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
  • Sources indicate that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

Sources indicate that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

It took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

At first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

According to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

Sources indicate that tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

As Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold latest routes here.

Industry observers note that according to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

Latest Update: We Tested the Shimano Sustain FK Spinning Reel in Fresh and Salt Water

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Recent findings suggest that the market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache.
  • Industry observers note that after all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

Recent findings suggest that the market is cluttered with spinning reels, and sorting through them to find one that meets specific needs can be a headache. That is especially true in light-tackle and inshore fishing, easily the most popular market for spinning reel manufacturers. At first glance, many reels in the 2500-size class, the standard size for this category, look identical. Appearances can be deceiving, though, and knowing how and where you strategy to use a reel matters more in this class than in most others.

Industry observers note that after all, why spend almost $400 on a 2500-size spinning reel that looks and feels about the same in hand as one that costs a quarter of the price? It turns out there are plenty of reasons, and Shimano makes the case for most of them with its updated Sustain FK series.

The Sustain FK gets its strength and light weight from Hagane metal body technology, a process of cold-forging rigid metals such as aluminum and magnesium. As part of Shimano’s MagnumLite series, the metal frame is also paired with an ultralight CI4+ carbon rotor. The result is a reel that feels solid and strong where it should, while staying smooth and light in use.

The Sustain FK uses DuraCross, a relatively fresh drag system from Shimano. The idea is that precisely layered materials give the reel a smoother, longer-lasting drag than older materials such as felt. Inside, the reel uses S A-RB bearings, which are shielded and rust-resistant to keep debris out. That adds a layer of protection against sand and salt, which helps keep the reel working in the saltwater conditions it was built for. Shimano also uses what it calls X-Protect, essentially a labyrinth of barriers that makes it far more difficult for salt water or grit to reach the interior of the reel.

No reel is invincible to the hazards of extended saltwater use, but the Sustain FK has a number of features that make it well suited to the task. Corrosion-resistant materials in the frame and gearing, S A-RB sealed bearings and Shimano’s X-Protect design give this reel several strong defenses against the wear and tear of frequent saltwater exposure. Shimano also pairs the DuraCross drag with its Rigid Support Drag to give this small reel a surprisingly strong backbone. The DuraCross drag in particular is a serious upgrade from the standard felt or carbon washers of previous models.

Shimano offers a one-year service warranty on its reels, including the Sustain FK. After that year, you can still send the reel in for service, and Shimano will usually inspect it and tell you the cost before doing the work. Experiences vary, but I’ve sent reels to Shimano countless times over the years and have found its warranty and service system easy to deal with and accommodating.

Shimano touts the Sustain FK as a crossover reel for fresh water and inshore salt water, with a combination of light finesse and rigid durability suited to both. With that in mind, I fished it in a wide range of environments over the course of a year, from bass fishing on large lakes and rivers with a variety of techniques to inshore saltwater fishing that ranged from shallow flats to deep near-shore jigging. The goal was to see whether it could stand up to the all-purpose abuse dished out by hardcore anglers nationwide while still delivering the refinement and finesse expected of a top-end spinning reel in the age of forward-facing sonar. Fishing from both boats and kayaks, I caught largemouth and smallmouth bass, redfish, striped bass and speckled trout.

Recent findings suggest that corrosion will always be the No. 1 concern when using any reel in salt water, especially one as small and lightweight as the Sustain FK 2500. To get a proper idea of how this reel holds up, I spent the better part of a year fishing with it from my kayak in places like Chesapeake Bay and Laguna Madre in Texas.

Recent findings suggest that A kayak is a great place to test how a reel holds up to the salt because the reel gets so much more direct exposure. Spray tends to reach reels sitting in kayak rod holders, and splashing water is much closer to your gear during high-intensity moments like fighting fish or navigating heavy current. Then there are the times anglers (myself included) accidentally submerge their gear when they aren’t paying attention.

So, how did the Sustain FK hold up? Remarkably well, I’m pleased to say. After roughly eight months of consistent, heavy saltwater use, the reel is still about as smooth as the day I opened it. It needs some basic maintenance, such as a freshwater rinse and a coat of reel oil now and then, but overall, I’m very impressed.

Sources indicate that smoothness matters, but a viable saltwater spinning reel needs a lot more than that. Saltwater game fish are bigger, stronger and live in harsher environments than most freshwater species, and a light spinning reel needs the backbone to stand up to that kind of abuse regularly without losing function. This is where the Sustain FK impressed me most. I intentionally used it in situations where the odds of hooking fish well outside its class were high, and I was able to fight and land everything from bull redfish to large striped bass around heavy cover without the reel bending or warping. The drag may be the reel’s best feature. It stayed smooth and clean during long runs that would have fried the drag on many reels in its class. The Rigid Support system was just as impressive. A reel this light will typically flex under that much strain, but the Sustain FK stayed rigid and smooth.

Ultimately, the Sustain FK passed every saltwater test with flying colors.

Industry observers note that being able to land saltwater fish well outside its intended class is great, but a high-end spinning reel should perform best at what it is intended for. That means no hiccups with anti-reverse or drag slippage, and handling line twist and line lay well. Today, it also means having the fine-tuning required for the extremely finesse-oriented game of fishing with forward-facing sonar. Love it or hate it, forward-facing sonar has become a standard part of professional angling, especially in the bass world.

With all that in mind, I used the Sustain FK for a wide range of freshwater applications. It performed well in traditional settings like fishing light jigs for river smallmouth bass and crappie, but that’s admittedly not a demanding test. Where this reel really shone was targeting bass on large, deep lakes where finesse and control at depth were key. Fishing with and without forward-facing sonar, I was impressed with the amount of control I could keep on the lure. From jerkbaits to small soft plastics, it never faltered with line management or fine-tuned movements.

The anti-twist fin that Shimano builds into the line roller on many of its high-end reels may sound like a gimmick, but trust me, it makes a massive difference. There’s not much worse than light braid twisting while you try to make long casts or present a bait at depth. It can cause wind knots and a host of other complications. Throughout testing, the line on this reel never kinked, twisted or laid poorly on the spool.

Finally, while the smooth, strong drag is great in salt water, the ability to fine-tune it is even more impressive for finesse fishing in fresh water. Getting a solid hook set in deep water on leader as light as 6-pound test can be critical for serious anglers, and that requires a drag that doesn’t slip or freeze up. The Sustain FK drag can be adjusted to the most minute settings, allowing for just the right resistance when setting the hook or playing fish on light line.

Sources indicate that I can’t remember using a reel that was as much at home fishing ultralight for crappie and perch as it was fishing a marsh for drag-ripping bull redfish and striped bass. I may be in the minority, but I love having a lightweight 2500-size spinning reel that pulls double duty as both my favorite freshwater finesse setup and my favorite inshore spinning rig. The crossover ability of the Sustain FK is fantastic. It’s not just a good freshwater reel that’s decent in the salt, or a saltwater reel that’s light enough to use in fresh water. It’s at the top of its game in both.

It has been revealed that the Sustain FK is an exceptional reel, so finding areas for improvement is difficult. The most obvious is the price. The engineering and performance can justify it, but there’s no denying that nearly $400 for a light spinning reel is steep for the average angler. There are plenty of equally light and smooth spinning reels on the market for far less. Those reels may not match the Sustain FK’s quality and durability across the board, but those features probably don’t matter as much to many freshwater or casual inshore anglers.

If you’re looking for a light-tackle spinning reel that’s durable and strong while still being incredibly smooth and light, the Sustain FK is the ideal choice. It’s comfortable to fish in both fresh and salt water, with the refinement needed for the most finesse-oriented applications.

It has been revealed that this review focused on the 2500, but the Sustain FK at the moment comes in sizes from 2500 through 5000. The limited size range is a downside, but given that this reel is designed for such a specific level of performance, it makes sense to offer it only in sizes that don’t compromise that.

Read Next: The Best Fishing Kayaks.

Although the price tag isn’t cheap, this reel is the complete package for serious anglers who want professional-grade performance from their gear. Tournament bass anglers and hardcore inshore anglers alike will appreciate the refinement the Sustain FK delivers over similar-size, budget-friendly options.

#91229. Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

📖 Baca

Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1221 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Senate prepares to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.
  • Recent findings suggest that the complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections.
  • BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the U.S. Senate prepares to vote this week on a bill aimed at easing America’s affordability crisis and fighting climate change that hunting and fishing groups worry will also erode many of the nation’s bedrock conservation laws.

Recent findings suggest that the complex and winding 400-page Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act focuses on lowering energy costs, something both Republicans and Democrats have championed and and that helped drive Democratic gains in the midterm elections. BAAJA also, however, ties jobs and household bills with curtailing public-lands protections. And in a twist that’s perplexing many conservation groups, the bill is co-sponsored by Sens. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) and Mike Lee (R-Utah), two lawmakers known for being on nearly opposite ends of the public-lands spectrum.

BAAJA is largely focused on permitting reform, something the country hasn’t tackled in decades, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center. In practice, the legislation would raise the standard for whether projects approved by one administration can be revoked by a future administration.

In a recent development, that means an industrial solar project permitted by one president, for example, could not be stymied by a future president intent on preventing renewables. It also speeds up permitting processes and cuts red tape for everything from energy projects to landscape-scale changes like prescribed fire.

According to recent reports, but sportsmen and conservationists say the bill would not just expedite climate or environmentally friendly projects. BAAJA would also make it much harder — or potentially impossible — for an administration to overturn leases or approvals for projects as controversial as hyperscale data centers on public lands or mines in the same watersheds as sensitive wilderness areas. It’s a bill that prioritizes development, many observers say, at the cost of the very “red tape” that has been responsible for conserving many of the country’s most priceless fish, wildlife, and wild places.

“I understand this is a massive, bipartisan bill — it has some things in it I would rather it not have. But I negotiated the deal based on what was actually possible to get signed into law,” Heinrich wrote in an email to Outdoor Life. “Because when I say climate change is an existential threat, I mean it. And I will not let an opportunity to do something about it pass by.”.

Conservationists like Ingrid Lyons, executive director of Save the Boundary Waters, understand the need for stability around permitting development. The whiplash between issuing and revoking permits for public land development projects every time an administration changes has likely hurt the U.S.’s ability to move forward with important energy projects, including in renewables like wind and solar.

But she fears this bill could instead cement the creation of controversial projects like a copper-sulfide mine at the headwaters of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness or a copper-molybdenum-gold mine in the salmon-rich waters of Alaska’s Bristol Bay. Permits for projects like these have been denied, among other concerns, because of environmental risk. If permits are reissued in similar scenarios, legislation like BAAJA could prevent future administrations from stopping development in places that truly need protection.

According to recent reports, “What about landscape certainty?” Lyons says. “We’re overlooking in some ways the impact to communities that are relying on protection and not just projects.”.

The conservation community has become increasingly vocal in its opposition to the bill since Heinrich and Lee partnered with Sens. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), and Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), to introduce the legislation in late September. Lee has a clear track record of supporting public land sales and undermining existing public-lands conservation, including 2025’s attempt to include federal land sales in the One Substantial Beautiful Bill.

A lengthy version of BAAJA is before the Senate as of Tuesday. The current bill includes a variety of red flags for hunters, anglers, tribes, endangered-species advocates, and other conservationists.

Some of the main points include:.

The Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership acknowledged the need for permit reform but said in a statement that “progress should not come at the expense of the conservation safeguards and public review that give hunters and anglers a voice in how our lands and waters are managed.”.

For Lyons, it comes down to the potential unintended consequences of sweeping legislation like BAAJA.

“We need to be exceptionally aware of the implications of this bill, which could be that a lot of these really beloved places could have projects many communities have worked really hard to oppose cemented into place.”.

Many in the conservation community were surprised by the bill’s sponsors, given Heinrich’s history as a sportsman and conservationist who regularly defends public lands and sensitive places, and Lee’s general position as a proponent of development and public-lands sell-off.

But in Heinrich’s statement to Outdoor Life, he emphasizes the impact of climate change on our planet, including the places where people hunt, hike, bike and camp. Independent modeling, he mentioned, predicts the bill will lead to a 20 percent reduction in power sector emissions, or the “equivalent to taking 39 coal plants offline for 10 years.”.

Recent findings suggest that “You cannot protect a trout stream without paying attention to the warming temperatures and declining flows that threaten it,” he wrote. “You cannot protect wildlife habitat while ignoring the impacts of increasingly severe drought and wildfire. We need to reduce emissions, and that means getting more clean energy onto the grid.”.

In a recent development, in an Oct. 30 op-ed in the Albuquerque Journal, Heinrich explained how New Mexico’s SunZia Wind and Transmission project took 17 years to permit and build.

He also pushed back on what he called misinformation about the bill, stating he doesn’t believe data centers should be on public land. The bill also requires large scale data center operators to pay the full cost of electricity consumed by the facility.

It has been revealed that the Izaak Walton League’s conservation director, Kate Miller, thinks each of the bill’s sponsors are acting in good faith and trying to do what is right for their constituents. Many projects, including those aimed at restoring forests and wildlife habitat, have been held up by permitting delays. Something like BAAJA could move those forward.

But Miller would have liked to see these challenges tackled individually instead of in a massive bill. And while she hopes that, if the bill passes, the administration will respect existing laws, the past two years has brought an onslaught of changes to most of the nation’s bedrock environmental laws including the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Environmental Policy Act.

It has been revealed that “We want to make sure what comes out is not something that sacrifices those core protections that allow us to have healthy waters and habitats,” Miller indicates. “That we don’t sacrifice one for the other.”.

Read Next: Alaska Considers ‘Unprecedented’ Closure of Public Land to Hunting, Trapping Along Controversial Ambler Road.

While the Senate is fast tracking the bill before the next Congress begins in January, it must move through the Senate and the House, and any changes be agreed upon by both chambers before the bill would land on President Trump’s desk. Meanwhile, both industry and conservation groups say they’re working to lobby lawmakers for changes and amendments. As a result, several conservation organizations declined to comment for this story.

#91228. Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2820 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Bear Tracks All Over the Arizona Trail

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2820 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that this morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail.
  • Recent findings suggest that by the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while.
  • Industry observers note that the views this morning were unbelievable.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this morning we woke up bright and early at our tent site right beside the trail. I was really hoping that we were going to get surprised last night by Leaf at some point, but she never did wind up catching up to us. At least today she’ll be heading into town from a trailhead less than 20 miles from where we were camped. So, she isn’t too far from a road, a town, and some hiking friends. I made coffee this morning pretty early and then laid in my tent for a while. Then the two of us got packed up and were walking on the trail before the sun was up. There isn’t too much awaiting us along the trail up ahead. Today we will be going past that major trailhead and highway crossing about 19 miles into the day. But other than that, it is just going to be us and the trail for the next few days. Depending on how far we go today and tomorrow, we’ll hopefully be able to head into town the following evening to resupply and recharge.

A small bear track in the muddy red clay.

Recent findings suggest that by the time the sun came up this morning we had already been walking for a while. And the trail actually had some fun surprises for us. Thanks to all of the rain, the trail had been covered in mud for the last couple of days. Which meant that any animal that hiked through the area would leave deep footprints in the trail. We got to follow the path of a bear which had been walking through this area in the last couple of days. It left behind such clear footprints in the red clay mud. It was cool to see the larger prints left behind by its back feet. This section of the trail was beautiful all on its own, but the prints in the mud added something special to it all.

Industry observers note that the views this morning were unbelievable. After all of the rain the red clay has the most incredible, deep color to it. And all of the trees and plants are vibrant and lush.

For the first hour or two of the day the trail was a dark red clay, complimented quite well by the lush pine trees and other shrubs surrounding the trail. The rising sun lit up the rocky mountainside off in the distance and made the red clay glow. That was a stunning way to start off the morning. We had some gradual climbing to do and continued to see bear prints along the trail on and off. If I was a bear, I would also love to follow the trail. It is a perfect path through the wilderness! It’s also one reason why some hikers prefer to set up their camp a little way off the trail at night. In the night, the trail is an animal highway through the woods. You never know what you’ll see if you follow a trail through the dark.

According to recent reports, I liked the way that the layer of clouds off in the distance was resting right above the mountain range. The Arizona Trail sure had a lot of trees today!

In a recent development, lucky for us, the mud wasn’t too bad this morning. Most of the moisture had been sucked in to the earth already. Leaving behind only the deep, saturated color that the water left behind. These sections of red clay are some of my favorites here in Arizona. The color looks incredible right beside the deep greens that we are able to enjoy thanks to all of the rain. I’ve had a lot of people reach out to say that the red clay typically doesn’t look nearly as vibrant as it does right now. All of the rain makes the color all the deeper, which I’m quite thankful for.

One particular stretch of trail that walked along a large red rock hillside.

Sources indicate that over the course of the morning the trail was following along a large cluster of rocks off in the distance. Some of them were shaped like tall, jagged chimneys. I really enjoyed the view as we got even closer to the rocks, before eventually the trail veered off. We actually ran into some people on the trail today as well. There are a ton of road crossings and trailhead throughout this area. One guy was out doing some trail maintenance scouting. I’m sure that the individuals doing trail maintenance through this area have their work cut out for them with all of the rain and flash flooding. An entire section of trail can so easily get washed away if enough water pours through an area. We’ve been lucky so far with the state of the trail. But there have definitely been a lot of sections and areas with fresh rock fall.

Industry observers note that clouds starting to roll in off in the distance. I thought we were going to get poured on! But as we stood on top of a ridge, we could see the storm blowing off and away from us.

By the late morning the temperature dropped a bit, and some dark clouds began to roll in. I hadn’t seen any rain in the forecast, but it certainly seemed like we had some coming for us. We stopped on top of a hill for a quick break, and each put our rain gear on while we watched it pour down off in the distance. It made me think about Leaf behind us, and all of our friends up ahead of us. The storm managed to skirt right on by us, and it hardly rained more than a sprinkle. But we could tell that someone somewhere was getting rained on. It felt nice to keep the rain gear on as we continued along, at least for a little while. We watched as the bulk of the storm blew by us and the skies got bright and blue off in the distance up ahead.

For a mile or two the trail slowly approached this cluster of unique rocks. A couple of them look like stone pillars.

Sources indicate that as we got closer to the trailhead and highway crossing, we did wind up getting rained on a bit. Which was surprising because the rain started just as the skies turned blue! It was only a sprinkle though. I used my sun umbrella to stay dry and the rain passed rapidly. Though, even just a light rain caused the mud on the trail to build back up again. I’m just hoping that the mud won’t be too bad for the rest of the day. Prior to reaching the trailhead, we ran into a couple more day hikers and one person on horseback with another horse being pulled behind them. The second horse had the cutest little pink saddle on. Then it wasn’t long until we reached the trailhead as well.

These bright yellow wildflowers have been growing all along the trail.

Arizona Trail signs near the trailhead about 20 miles into our day.

For some reason it always feels exciting to pass by a trailhead, even if you aren’t heading into town. Perhaps it’s the possibility of receiving some trail magic there or having something else eventful occur. When we actually passed by the trailhead though there was hardly anyone around and we just continued along. And we only made it another mile or two before we encountered the next obstacle ahead of us. There was another deep river crossing for us to ford! This one was quite easy in comparison to our river crossing yesterday. We walked around to see if there was any way that we could avoid getting our feet wet, but there was not. So, we both plunged in and got our shoes and socks soaked. Then sat on the other side of the river to enjoy a lunch break.

After Slide and I crossed the river, we sat here in the grass to eat lunch.

The sky was still dark off in the distance and it certainly felt like it was going to rain at some point. Both of us figured this would be a good time to stop and eat, just in case the rain did start up. I had packed out one of those tasty bite tikka masala meals which I enjoyed there. Those always do a great job of filling me up. Then I cleaned out my socks and shoes and debated on whether or not I should put my rain gear back on. We were going to begin going uphill, so I knew I was going to get super-hot in rain gear. But if it’s windy at all then I still get wet when I’m using just my umbrella. I decided to opt against it and just figured that if the rain did start and was heavy, I could just stop and put my rain jacket on later.

In the early evening the trail briefly followed along this massive slab of rock. It reminded me of sections of the Appalachian Trail in Fresh York.

Industry observers note that the rain wound up holding off as we continued along. It sprinkled on us briefly but didn’t persist. Once we left the river, we did have a bit of climbing to do. Then we were up on top of the nearby hill and just continued along up there. In some places the trail itself was just a massive boulder beneath the ground. We had some open and exposed views, and the weather was nice and cool. It felt like we had gotten pretty lucky already for the day. It wouldn’t be long before I had to get my feet wet again in yet another small stream crossing. I probably could have tried harder and kept my feet dry, but it felt like a lot of work. I also always have the strong memory in my mind of slipping on a rock in a river crossing in Northern California on the PCT and breaking 2 of my fingers last year. All to avoid getting my feet wet! I actually wound up getting more wet than I would have if I just crossed through the river normally, because I slipped and fell. Of course, at the time I didn’t realize that I’d broken 2 of my fingers. But 4 months later I still couldn’t apply any pressure to the two fingers on my right hand, so it feels like a safe assumption now.

A photo that Slide took of me when we were on top of this ridge. The trail stayed up there for the rest of the evening and the views just got better and better.

Industry observers note that as we continued along the trail was pretty rocky, but in exchange we were graced with some great views. The trail went through some areas with vibrant foliage as well. The leaves were a perfect spectrum of light greens, yellows, oranges, and deep reds. It reminds me so much of hiking in Colorado this time of year. We even saw a bunch more bear prints along the trail over the course of the evening. And some prints that appeared to be a large dog. They definitely didn’t look like mountain lion prints, in my opinion. I’m not sure what else they could be besides a dog!

I figured these were just significant dog prints, but I still like the way that they looked in the mud.

Recent findings suggest that by the time that the sun began to set we were up top of a ridge and would be continuing along it for the rest of the evening. The sun cast an incredible glow across the wheat grass and other plants surrounding the trail. There were loads of bright yellow wildflowers and prickly pear cacti throughout the area as well. It was a really beautiful way to end off the day. Sometime after 5PM we passed my favorite bear prints of the entire day. There were some prints which were incredibly deep and had standing water inside of them. It just really highlighted how massive the prints were. I wonder where this bear was going, and if it was the same bear whose prints we saw earlier on in the day. I’m sure it’s not, but bears can travel very far in a day if they want to.

Perfectly defined bear prints right on the trail.

In the early evening, we entered into the Mazatzal Wilderness in the Tonto National Forest. At this point the sun was just starting to go down, and the sky was putting on quite the show for us. The trail got much rockier in this section and there were way more cacti lining the trail as well. The timing wasn’t great, because we would be looking for camping sometime soon. When the trail is lined in rocks and cacti it can be hard to find a place to set up your tent. As we walked, I snacked on some pistachios and enjoyed the views. We were in the perfect place to be able to enjoy the sunset this evening.

The sun was beginning to set, and we were in the perfect place to enjoy it.

Sources indicate that the trail stayed pretty much the same for the rest of the night. There were rocks all over the place and a ton of cacti. Camping options seemed limited at best, if not nonexistent. But we just kept our eyes peeled for any area with less rocks and some flat ground. Just after it got dark, we did wind up finding an area just off the trail which didn’t seem too bad. It was a little rocky and lumpy but was definitely much better than what we had been seeing. It was hard to imagine that we would find anything much better than this anytime soon. So, we decided to just call it a day then and there. We both got our tents set up, and it was a great feeling to take off my shoes and socks. They weren’t soaked, but they definitely weren’t dry. The worst part about wet shoes and socks, in opinion, is putting them back on the next morning. Especially when it is cold out! It could take my breath away.

Enjoying that last bit of light before the sun completely dipped behind the mountains off in the distance.

In a recent development, once my tent was up, I got comfortable inside and ate something. Then did my stretching routine before calling it a night. We made it 31 miles today which was pretty good. Sure, we could have gone a bit further to make our life easier tomorrow and the next day. But we certainly didn’t need to. I think we’ll wind up having another early start tomorrow morning which will make up for it. There is a ton of elevation gain tomorrow, so I’m curious to see how that goes.

If you enjoyed this blog and would like to support my hike by buying me a soda or a snack along the way, there is a “Tip the Author” button below! It links directly to my Venmo. Any and all support is incredibly appreciated!

The tall wheatgrass looked almost pink under the glow of those cotton candy clouds.

This was easily one of the best views that I’ve had the pleasure of enjoying thus far on the Arizona Trail. The sunsets and sunrises out here have been fantastic.

Industry News: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Takes Plea Deal After Poaching 6×6 Bull Elk, Trespassing

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (508 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.
  • According to recent reports, on Nov.
  • His guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Idaho Fish and Game commissioner just made a deal to avoid poaching and trespassing charges related to an illegal elk hunt last season.

According to recent reports, on Nov. 9 eastern Idaho’s representative, Brody Harshbarger, agreed to plead guilty to two of seven charges of wildlife violations in exchange for having the remaining charges dropped.

His guilty pleas are for hunting without a tag and shooting across the road, according to local news outlets. The dismissed charges include two for poaching, trespass, motorized aid and failure to retrieve game. Both of the killed animals were bull elk, one antlerless and the other a 6×6 which was on private property. Harshbarger was accompanied by another man, Eric Murphy, at the time.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Notes He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

It has been revealed that “Neither Brody Harshbarger nor Eric Murphy called the landowners to request permission to retrieve the six-point bull and did not make a reasonable effort to retrieve the six-point bull,” according to investigation documents obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Neither individual had permission to be shooting onto the private property in violation of Idaho Code.”.

Harshbarger had already filled his elk tag the weekend before the two bulls were shot. His hometown, Ashton, is in the same county where the violations took place. That same county, Fremont, borders Yellowstone National Park and is in the region Harshbarger represents on the state’s seven-person commission. That commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists.

Each member of the commission, most often a resident hunter and/or fisherman, is appointed by the governor for a term of four years with a two-term maximum. The commission meets at least four times a year. Harshbarger hasn’t attended those meetings since his case opened after a tip received through the department’s Citizens Against Poaching in December. He hasn’t resigned and the Governor hasn’t dismissed him, but his profile has been removed from the commission’s website.

“The Governor’s office is aware of Commissioner Harshbarger’s plea agreement,” Gov. Brad Little’s spokeswoman Emily Callihan told the Sun. “Gov. Little will be working with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game and stakeholders in the coming days to ensure the responsibilities of the position are fulfilled.”.

Sources indicate that harshbarger was appointed to the commission in 2024. His sentencing for illegal activities in 2025 is scheduled for Dec. 9. With the fresh plea deal and the number of charges reduced, the fine is expected to be $500 plus a one-year loss of hunting privileges.

Read Next: DNA Evidence Helps Convict Serial Poacher, Who Forfeited 2 Vehicles and Hunting Privileges for Life.

CAP received 1,596 calls about illegal wildlife-related activity in 2025, the highest on record since an annual total started rolling in 2019. A tip about a poached elk that leads to an arrest is worth $400. CAP rewarded tipsters more than $23,000 in 2025.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

According to recent reports, the storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

“That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

Recent findings suggest that driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

Recent findings suggest that with hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

Up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better company but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

Sources indicate that timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

Recent findings suggest that in Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

It has been revealed that gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

According to recent reports, the reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the new windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

Sources indicate that it’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies.
  • This summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks.
  • Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jeff Sturgis has made a name for himself by helping deer hunters and property owners better understand habitat and high-level hunting strategies. He’s honed these strategies through decades of hard hunting and consulting on his clients’ properties. He’s also tested them on his own 170-acre property in the bluff country of southern Minnesota (you can follow him on his YouTube channel, Whitetail Habitat Solutions).

This summer, I got to visit Sturgis’ property and get a high-level overview of how he thinks about habitat and targeting mature bucks. In the video above, Sturgis runs through his five favorite setups and explains how he hunts them. Some of these setups take an immense amount of work and expense to develop. Others require minimal habitat work but a deep understanding of deer behavior.

Whether or not you are able to build these exact setups on your own hunting area, there are some key lessons you can learn from him.

Everyone talks about “buck bedding areas” but many hunters have only a vague understanding of them. The important point, Sturgis indicates, is that bucks do not like to bed near a lot of commotion, and that includes commotion from other deer. For example, does will often bed near major food sources. It’s convenient for them to get up from their bed and stroll right into a large food plot or ag field.

Recent findings suggest that mature bucks don’t like to bed around a mass of other deer. So buck beds will be found farther away from main food sources — even if there is prime bedding habitat right by those food sources. So just because you’re seeing a lot of does and young bucks in an area doesn’t mean it’s a good spot for mature bucks. In fact, it could mean the opposite.

Sources indicate that by crossing off areas where mature bucks won’t bed — again, areas with high pressure and activity — you can narrow down where they will bed. Sturgis isn’t afraid to hunt near buck bedding areas, but he does so sparingly. And when he does, he often takes his target buck.

According to recent reports, when you see deer consistently coming to a substantial food plot or agricultural field during daylight hours, it’s tempting to just hunt that major food source. Sturgis will hunt the big “holding plot” on his property, but only when he’s able to do so without spooking deer. He’s got a Redneck blind at the edge of the plot, which has an access route that is completely blocked by screening cover. He can get into and out of the blind with deer in the field — and never spook them. But that setup means he’s only able to hunt the big holding plot during gun season, even if there are target bucks hitting it during bow season.

Sturgis considers the holding plot the cornerstone of his entire property. So long as deer feel safe feeding there, he’s in the game. Even if he happens to bump a buck out of its bedding area, that deer is likely to switch bedding areas but still come to the holding plot to feed. This means that Sturgis can keep hunting that buck.

On the flipside, if he blows out the holding plot, it throws off deer behavior for the entire property, and that could be detrimental to his entire season. In some ways, he treats the holding plot like a sanctuary.

Sources indicate that sturgis has a ton of videos about how to set up and hunt waterholes. He creates his waterhole setups in the woods in traditional rut funnels. These waterholes give deer a reason to come within bow range and to stop there. Sturgis and his wife, Jen, have some of their best significant-buck hunts over waterholes.

These setups are relatively easy to implement, assuming you can get some kind of water tank into the woods where you hunt. They’re great places for all-day sits during the heart of the rut.

Sources indicate that we all love to be in the woods before sunrise and to hear the telltale sound of a buck marching into range just after shooting light. But in some cases it’s impossible to hunt a spot first thing in the morning without spooking deer. These are often areas near field edges — deer are still in the fields feeding in the dark.

In these scenarios Sturgis will simply enter the stand an hour or so after daylight when deer have left the field. This allows him to slip in undetected and have several hours of quality hunting before leaving again in the evening. These are usually high-probability sits during the rut.

The main principle that Sturgis’ hunting strategy revolves around is to not overpressure mature deer. He wants big bucks to do their thing: rut, establish their dominance, and move around the habitat, during daylight hours. He lets his Tactacam trail cameras do the monitoring, and he picks his sits carefully. Of course we all love being in the woods and Sturgis does too. So he has stands that are very low impact for those times when he or someone in his family just wants to hunt — and you never know, a mature buck could stroll by any time.

But his approach is much more surgical when really targeting a specific deer.

Sources indicate that one of the many things I learned from Sturgis is that all of the knowledge (and much more) outlined above has been built into the Habitat IQ app. This app allows the user to draw in habitat features (like food sources, water, timber, and roads) into their own property. The program then uses a powerful algorithm, built off of Sturgis’ knowledge, to make habitat improvement suggestions and predict deer movement.

For example, if you don’t have any useful water sources on your property, the app will suggest adding some waterholes, and give you an idea about the best areas to place them.

Related: Here’s What Most Hunters Get Wrong About Whitetails, According to Jeff Sturgis.

Recent findings suggest that the app is basically a digital version of Sturgis’ habitat/hunting consulting business. The more data you add into it, the better information you get back. I think this will be an incredibly powerful tool for anyone who is looking to implement the concepts that Sturgis has proven out over the course of 20-plus years of consulting on deer properties.

#91217. Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1306 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Why am I’m Hiking?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1306 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.
  • There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.
  • I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

So, the question I usually get from people when I tell them I’m hiking the Appalachian Trail is, “Why?”.

There’s a lot of emotion behind that question, and it can lead to very different answers.

I could talk about the people who ask with frustration, disbelief, sadness, or even fear. Maybe they’re worried that the things I normally handle will now fall into their laps. Then there are the people who sound surprised or curious. I may have to explain exactly what backpacking is and what thru-hiking entails. Those conversations lead to a whole different brand of questions. These are the best discussions, and I can go down all kinds of rabbit holes about gear, food, concerns about animals, and where I’m going to sleep.

Sources indicate that the question, though, is still this: Why am I going to hike for six months, leaving a perfectly good couch, bed, wife, career, and a couple of affectionate cats behind? All to be cold, wet, and worn out most days from doing nothing but walking? Miles and miles of walking.

I have to go way back, maybe 14 years ago, when my wife and I were exposing the kids to all kinds of different vacations, ideally the kind that didn’t cost much. For several years, we had been camping at National Parks, enjoying the sights and activities. One of those years, when we were in the Rockies, we saw a young couple leaving camp with their tiny kids, each carrying an even tinier backpack. We remembered a couple of backpacking trips we’d taken after we got married but before we had kids. The gear had been sitting on a shelf for years, but at least we still had some.

“Let’s take the kids next year!”.

The next year, we suited up. Our kids now had their own tiny packs. We had food, fuel, and ponchos in case it rained.

Did I mention we were on a small section of the Appalachian Trail in the Smoky Mountains?

It rained for three days straight before we even started our hike, and then it rained for the three days we were on the trail. Thankfully, we stayed in shelters, but there were a lot of lessons learned. Lessons about food, clothing, footwear, water treatment and yes, raingear. Still, I came off the trail with a huge smile. Can’t say that about the kids, but for me, I had a blast! Spoiler – both my kids are now young adults and camp, sometimes willingly but I’m getting distracted.

Industry observers note that the biggest lesson for me came when we got off the trail. My daughter pointed to the large sign behind me that mentioned “Appalachian Trail” which told me about its more than 2,150 miles of hiking that people tackle every year.

Pretty sure my response was, “That’s ridiculous. No one can do that.” The food, if nothing else, would weigh hundreds of pounds, not to mention all the fuel we’d need to boil water. It would take an Ironman-caliber person just to carry all of that.

Recent findings suggest that somewhere around there, I started going down the rabbit hole of research. Resupply every few days? Okay. That’s feasible. Water filters? That would save a lot of time compared to hours of boiling water (which, yes, we had been doing). Lighter-weight gear? I could do that.

I fell in love with the concept of it.

Industry observers note that so why? Why would I spent 6 months in the woods hiking?

It has been revealed that it wasn’t the romantic feel of trail life (though a lot of trail journals do talk very positively about it). I could talk about my love of nature and wanting to be out in the woods, watching the slow change of the seasons. That isn’t completely it. I can do that from my bedroom window. I could mention making newly introduced friends or reducing the clutter in my life. I could learn that last lesson by just going to my parents’ house and looking at the hoarding nightmare in their basement that’s slowly becoming my problem. All key things and outcomes I’ve read about from other hikers.

Sources indicate that no, I think for me, I fell in love with the idea of an adventure. One that would be within my grasp as a middle-aged, desk-jockey engineer who really needed some outdoor time to recharge his batteries before returning to the world of engineering work. Not quite ready for retirement, but not wanting to spend all my years letting my glutes go to crap while I sit in a chair and pound on a keyboard, arguing over engineering details with team members spread out across the globe while we work toward a common, fresh design.

In a recent development, I don’t picture it as some grand adventure of heading off at sunrise, marching to Mordor with a ring, or even trekking through the wilderness to find myself. But I do want to have an adventure that, as I get older, I can fondly stare off into space remembering… remembering the tough days, the worn-out feelings, the beautiful views, the green tunnel, latest friendships, and new experiences.

Industry observers note that that’s why I’m heading out to the woods for six months. It’s not to run away from legal trouble (I don’t even have any overdue parking tickets). It’s not to flee from my job (I actually do like what I’m doing, but after thirty-plus years, a break would be nice). It’s not to escape from my family (I happen to like them, too. Well, most of the time, but I’m sure that feeling is mutual).

Recent findings suggest that so, if I had to state the biggest, single reason, it’s because I’m looking to have an adventure, one where the journey is the destination. And if I can make it to Katahdin with a bunch of new friends and great stories, all the better.

The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

About me? Sure. I’m a native Detroiter and have lived my whole life in Michigan where I live with my wife – more than 25 years – and a couple of college-aged children. Well, technically the kids live off at college but they do come home to make the house look a natural disaster struck while we weren’t looking. I’m an engineer, working for one of the Substantial Three automakers and have well over 30 years of experience doing everything from breaking transmissions to quality improvements and even designing cooling systems for both trucks and cars. Outside of work, I love exploring and spending time outdoors. I’ve learned a lot about camping over the last few decades, including relearning wonderful lessons like not leaving an unlocked cooler in camp and proper flow directions on my water filter. Somewhere in there, I fell in love with backpacking and found a whole latest world of mistakes I can learn from. Eventually, I discovered long-distance thru-hiking and convinced both my job and my family that taking a vacation from me for six months would be beneficial to them (suckers!). Catch me on a good day, and I’d be happy to talk about camping, backpacking, video games, books, music or just about anything else fun. Just don’t ask me about spreadsheets, checklists, FMEAs or change control meetings.

Notify me via e-mail if anyone answers my comment.
